Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $M$. A family of smooth functions $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ with $\phi_i:M\to [0,1]$ is a **smooth partition of unity subordinate to** $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ when:

1. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i))_{i\in I}$ is locally finite;
2. $\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$; and
3. $\sum_i \phi_i(p)=1$ for every $p\in M$.

An **abstract simplicial complex** is a pair $(V,K)$ consisting of a set $V$ of
vertices and a family $K$ of finite subsets of $V$ such that:

1. $\varnothing \in K$;
2. if $\sigma \in K$ and $\tau \subseteq \sigma$, then $\tau \in K$;
3. every singleton $\{v\}$ with $v \in V$ lies in $K$.

The elements of $K$ are the **simplices** of the complex. If $\sigma \in K$ is
nonempty, its dimension is $\dim \sigma := |\sigma|-1$, and the empty simplex
has dimension $-1$.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization**
$|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that:

1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$;
2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$;
3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$.

For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write
$$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$
Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple
$(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric
simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so
$|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology.

We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions:
a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open
in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For arbitrary topological spaces $X,Y$, with $C_0(I,Y)$ carrying the ordinary compact-open topology, the assignments $H(x,t)=h(x)(t)$ give a bijection between continuous maps $X\times I\to Y$ and $X\to C_0(I,Y)$. If $q:X\to Q$ is an arbitrary quotient map, $q\times\mathrm{id}_I$ is an ordinary quotient map. For CG spaces the correspondence lifts to kified mapping spaces and respects based restrictions and homotopies. For CGWH targets the based mapping subspaces are CGWH.

derivations.claim: Define $f:M\to|N|$ by $f(x)=\sum_i\phi_i(x)i$. Its finite support consists of cover members containing $x$, so it spans a nerve simplex. The map is continuous for the weak realization topology: near a point only finitely many supports occur, and after shrinking the neighborhood every remaining assigned $U_i$ contains it. Thus the local map lands continuously in one finite simplex. Empty cover members contribute no vertex and may be omitted.

Define the barycentric subdivision $N'$ whose vertices are nonempty simplices $\sigma$ of $N$ and whose simplices are strict finite chains $\sigma_0\subset\cdots\subset\sigma_k$. The map $h:|N'|\to|N|$ sends the vertex $\sigma$ to its barycenter. It is a homeomorphism by an explicit simplexwise inverse: if a point has distinct positive coordinate levels $\lambda_1>\cdots>\lambda_r>0$, put $\sigma_j=\{i:t_i\ge\lambda_j\}$ and $\lambda_{r+1}=0$. Its expression is $\sum_j |\sigma_j|(\lambda_j-\lambda_{j+1})b_{\sigma_j}$. These nonnegative weights sum to one and recover each coordinate. When levels coincide the intervening weight becomes zero, and on a face zero coordinates disappear; hence the inverse is continuous on each closed simplex and for the weak topologies in [F3].

Using [A1], choose $x_\sigma\in U_\sigma$ for every nonempty simplex. Construct $g:|N'|\to M$ on a chain simplex recursively. Its vertex $\sigma$ maps to $x_\sigma$. For $\sigma_0\subset\cdots\subset\sigma_k$, cone the already defined opposite face to $x_{\sigma_0}$ using the unique minimizing geodesics in $U_{\sigma_0}$. The opposite face lies in $U_{\sigma_1}\subset U_{\sigma_0}$ by induction. The cone agrees with the constructions on all other faces because deleting a vertex leaves the same ordered coning formula. It is continuous at the cone point by compactness of each face image and smooth dependence of the convex geodesics in [F1]. The resulting map has image in $U_{\sigma_0}$ on this chain simplex and is globally continuous by the weak topology.

For $x\in M$, each simplex in the chain representing $h^{-1}f(x)$ is a face of the support simplex of $f(x)$. Thus both $x$ and $g h^{-1}f(x)$ lie in the same $U_{\sigma_0}$. Join them by its unique minimizing geodesic. This gives a homotopy $g h^{-1}f\simeq\operatorname{id}_M$. It is continuous even when the chain changes: on every convex-pair neighborhood geodesics depend continuously on both endpoints, and the local formulas agree on overlaps by uniqueness of the minimizing geodesic. No CW topology on a thick nerve is assumed.

We construct the other inverse homotopy by carriers. For the chain simplex with smallest face $\sigma_0$, let $C_{\sigma_0}$ be the subcomplex of nerve simplices $\tau$ for which $\tau\cup\sigma_0$ is a simplex. It contracts to $b_{\sigma_0}$ by straight barycentric interpolation. The map $h$ lies in this carrier, since its support is contained in the largest chain face; $f g$ lies there because $g$ lands in $U_{\sigma_0}$ and all members in the support of $f(g(-))$ contain that same point. A face of a chain either has the same smallest simplex or a larger one; its carrier is therefore contained in $C_{\sigma_0}$. Induct over chain-simplex dimension to homotope $fg$ to $h$ within these carriers. On a closed $k$-simplex, the two endpoint maps and the already fixed boundary homotopy define a map from the boundary of its prism into the contractible carrier. Extend across the prism by coning that boundary map with the displayed contraction. This extends the homotopy relative to all previously defined faces. For continuity, transpose each characteristic-prism map into the compact-open interval mapping space by [F6]. The maps agree on faces, so the weak topology of [F3] gives a continuous global transpose; untransposing by [F6] gives the required homotopy on the ordinary product with the interval. Consequently $f g h^{-1}\simeq\operatorname{id}_{|N|}$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $M\simeq|N|$ by actual inverse maps.

Simplicial and singular integral chains are free. Their natural comparison is a homology isomorphism by [F5]. Applying the natural cohomological universal-coefficient short exact sequences gives isomorphisms on the Ext and Hom terms, hence on cohomology by the elementary exact-sequence diagram argument. Therefore $H^*_{\mathrm{simp}}(N;\mathbb F_2)\cong H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(|N|;\mathbb F_2)$. The homotopy equivalence of step 4.1 identifies this with $H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb F_2)$. Two subordinate partitions give homotopic maps $f$ by convex interpolation: their combined support at $x$ consists entirely of sets containing $x$. For a refinement, the composed nerve map and the original partition map have the same property and are homotopic by the same interpolation. Thus the cohomology comparison is independent of those choices and natural under refinement; the choices of $g$ merely supply its inverse.

If $M$ is empty, the nerve has no nonempty simplex and both realizations/maps are empty. A singleton simplex is handled by its chosen point and the same geodesic contraction. Infinite covers cause no compact-image assumption on a thick realization: continuity follows simplexwise and local finiteness of the partition, and the homotopy is built on actual CW prisms. Full AC supplies the choices in [A1] and [F2]; no extra choice strength is introduced.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold of even dimension $2m$, and let $V=V^+\oplus V^-$ be a finite-rank smooth complex vector bundle with a Hermitian metric linear in its first variable. Write $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathbb C}(T^*M,-g)$ for the complex Clifford bundle generated by cotangent vectors with relation $\xi\eta+\eta\xi=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)$. A **graded Hermitian Clifford action** is a smooth real-linear map $c:T^*M\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ such that $c(\xi)^*=-c(\xi)$, $c(\xi)V^\pm\subseteq V^\mp$, and $c(\xi)c(\eta)+c(\eta)c(\xi)=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)I$. It extends complex-linearly to the complex Clifford bundle.

A **graded Hermitian Clifford connection** is a unitary connection $\nabla^V$ preserving $V^\pm$ and satisfying
$$\nabla^V_X(c(\xi)v)=c(\nabla^{LC}_X\xi)v+c(\xi)\nabla^V_Xv$$
for smooth $X,\xi,v$, where $\nabla^{LC}$ is the Levi–Civita connection. In a local orthonormal coframe $(e^i)$ define
$$D_Vv=\sum_i c(e^i)\nabla^V_{e_i}v.$$
The operator is odd, so its chiral part is $D_V^+:C^\infty(V^+)\to C^\infty(V^-)$. The formula's frame independence, formal symmetry on closed $M$, and global bundle well-definedness are proved in [[lem-geometric-dirac-operator-is-well-defined]]. A domain and index are assigned only under the compact hypotheses of later items.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth real vector bundle of rank $2r$, where $r\geq0$,
over a smooth manifold that may have boundary. A **smooth complex structure**
on $E$ is a smooth bundle endomorphism $J:E\to E$ with $J^2=-I$. It makes
each fiber a complex vector space by $(a+ib)v=av+bJv$. Equivalently, $E$ has
local smooth complex frames with transition maps in $\operatorname{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$. In one direction, multiplication by $i$ in complex bundle charts gives
such a smooth $J$ because the transition maps are complex-linear. Conversely,
near any point choose a complex basis in its fiber and extend its vectors to
local smooth real sections; those sections together with their $J$-images
remain a real frame after shrinking the neighborhood, and give a local complex
frame. Forgetting smoothness in these charts gives the associated rank-$r$
complex topological vector bundle of
[[def-real-and-complex-topological-vector-bundle]].

For a smooth complex bundle $(E,J)$, write $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)$ for its
smooth complex sections. A **complex connection** is a covariant derivative
$\nabla:\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(E)\to\Omega^1(M;E)$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear
and satisfies
$$\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\nabla s$$
for every smooth complex-valued function $f$ and section $s$. This extends the
real bundle-connection convention of
[[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. A complex connection is
**Hermitian** for a supplied Hermitian metric $h$, taken linear in its first
variable and conjugate-linear in its second, when
$$Xh(s,t)=h(\nabla_Xs,t)+h(s,\nabla_Xt)$$
for all smooth sections $s,t$ and vector fields $X$. A real connection on a
Euclidean vector bundle is **Euclidean-compatible** when it obeys the same
identity for the real bundle metric, as in
[[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]].

Assume countable choice. On an oriented Riemannian manifold with boundary, $n\ge1$, a smooth compactly supported vector field satisfies $\int_M(\operatorname{div}_gX)\operatorname{vol}_g=\int_{\partial M}g(X,\nu)\operatorname{vol}_{\partial g}$, with outward unit normal $\nu$ and outward-normal-first boundary orientation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

abla_{e'_i}=\sum_k a_{ik}

abla_{e'_i}=\sum_{i,j,k}a_{ij}a_{ik}c(e^j)
abla_{e_k}=\sum_jc(e^j)
abla_{e_j}$ by $\sum_i a_{ij}a_{ik}=\delta_{jk}$. Each chart expression has smooth coefficients, and these overlap equalities glue them to one global first-order operator.

Define the complex vector field $Y=\sum_i\langle c(e^i)u,vangle e_i$ for smooth sections $u,v$. At any chosen point take a local orthonormal frame with $
abla^{LC}e_i=0$ there. Using [F2], metric compatibility and $

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

Let $E\to M$ be a finite-rank smooth real vector bundle on a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold; manifolds with boundary are allowed. Write $\Gamma(E)$ for its smooth sections, as in [[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]. Define
$$\Omega^1(M;E)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Hom}(TM,E)).$$
The Hom bundle is the canonical smooth bundle constructed below from the supplied smooth tangent bundle and E. Thus an element $\eta$ assigns a linear map $\eta_p:T_pM\to E_p$ to each point, smoothly in bundle charts. This is also the meaning of an $E$-valued one-form, customarily written as a section of $T^*M\otimes E$. No tangent-only tensor construction is needed for this definition.

A **connection** on $E$ is an $\mathbb R$-linear map $\nabla:\Gamma(E)\to\Omega^1(M;E)$ such that, for every $f\in C^\infty(M)$ and $s\in\Gamma(E)$,
$$\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\nabla s.$$
Here $(df\otimes s)_p(v)=df_p(v)s(p)$, using [[def-differential-of-a-smooth-real-valued-function]]. In local coordinates and a local frame of $E$, this map has entries $(\partial_i f)s^a$, so it is a smooth Hom-bundle section. The tensor notation in the rule therefore already has a defined meaning.

This definition specifies a given operator, not its existence. The local operator rules and the Hom construction from supplied smooth bundles use no choice axiom. If $M$ is empty or $E$ has rank zero, both spaces are zero spaces and there is exactly one such operator. If $M$ has dimension zero, $TM$ is the zero bundle and the same conclusion holds, even when $E$ has positive rank. Rank one uses the same definition without a preferred trivialization.


**Smooth Hom bundles from supplied smooth bundles.** The following construction supplies the Hom notation used here and in the subsequent dual and tensor constructions. Let $A,B\to M$ be supplied smooth real vector bundles of ranks $r,s$, in the sense of [[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]], with Hausdorff second-countable total spaces. The same local product convention is used when $M$ has boundary. We construct the smooth structure on the fibrewise set $H=\coprod_{p\in M}\operatorname{Hom}(A_p,B_p)$, rather than infer global topology from transition matrices alone.

If $r,s>0$, let $D\subseteq A^r\times B^r$ consist of tuples $(a_1,\ldots,a_r,b_1,\ldots,b_r)$ over a common base point $p$ such that $(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ is a basis of $A_p$. Give $D$ the subspace topology of the finite product [[def-product-topology]]. Fix one countable base of each of the two supplied total spaces; this is a finite choice of witnesses in ZF, not a countable family of choices. Finite product boxes give a countable base of $A^r\times B^r$, because their indices lie in a finite product of countable sets, countable by repeated application of [[thm-product-of-countable]]. Taking traces gives a countable base of $D$ by [[prop-second-countability-is-hereditary]]. No manifold structure on that ambient product or its fibre-product subspace is needed.

Define $q:D\to H$ by sending a tuple to the unique linear map $a_i\mapsto b_i$. The map is onto: each individual finite-dimensional fibre has a basis, and a specified map determines the corresponding $b_i$; this pointwise existence does not choose bases simultaneously. Give $H$ the quotient topology [[def-quotient-topology]]. For any one common local trivialization of $A,B$ over $U$, the open saturated subspace $D_U$ is homeomorphic to $U\times GL(r,\mathbb R)\times M_{s\times r}(\mathbb R)$. Write its coordinates $(p,C,V)$, with the frame vectors the columns of $C$ and the image vectors the columns of $V$. The proposed Hom chart sends a fibre map to its matrix $T$ in the fixed local frames, and its composite with $q$ is
$$ (p,C,V)\longmapsto(p,VC^{-1}). $$
This map is a continuous open surjection: $(p,C,V)\mapsto(p,C,VC^{-1})$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $(p,C,T)\mapsto(p,C,TC)$, and projection off $GL(r,\mathbb R)$ is open, as is seen on product boxes. Smooth matrix inversion, in particular continuity, is supplied by [[lem-matrix-inversion-preserves-ck-regularity]]. Thus the composite is quotient by [[lem-open-or-closed-surjection-is-quotient]]. Since $D_U$ is open and saturated, the quotient criterion also says that $H_U$ is open and the restricted quotient topology agrees with its subspace topology. Comparing the two quotient criteria proves that the proposed Hom chart $H_U\to U\times M_{s\times r}(\mathbb R)$ is a homeomorphism.

These local formulas also prove that $q$ is globally open: for open $O\subseteq D$, its image intersected with every $H_U$ is the open image of $O\cap D_U$ in this chart. $\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

A $\mathbb K$-linear map $P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(E)$ is a **linear differential

If $2a>r+n/2$, Sobolev embedding bounds every $C^r$ norm by the same polynomial. The dimension of the spectral subspace $P\le L$ is polynomially bounded: point evaluation on that subspace has operator norm at most $C(1+L)^a$; summing its squared norm over an orthonormal basis and integrating over compact $M$ gives $\dim 1_{[0,L]}(P)L^2\le C'(1+L)^{2a}$.

The polynomial counting bound and the polynomial $C^r$ eigenfunction bounds imply $\sum_j e^{-t\lambda_j}(1+\lambda_j)^q<\infty$ for every fixed $t>0$ and integer $q$: split $[0,\infty)$ into dyadic shells, bound the number and $C^r$ norm on each shell polynomially, and use $e^{-t2^k}$ to dominate every polynomial. Thus $K_t(x,y)=\sum_j e^{-t\lambda_j}u_j(x)\otimes u_j(y)^*$ and every fixed space/time derivative converge absolutely and uniformly. The series solves $(\partial_t+P_x)K_t=0$, and integrating it against a smooth section gives $e^{-tP}$ by the orthonormal expansion. Termwise integration on the diagonal gives $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-tP})=\sum_j e^{-t\lambda_j}<\infty$.

On smooth sections $P_-D^+=D^+P_+$ and $D^-D^+=P_+$, $D^+D^-=P_-$. Thus for $\lambda>0$, $D^+$ maps its $P_+$ eigenspace isomorphically to the $P_-$ eigenspace with inverse $\lambda^{-1}D^-$, so their contributions to the graded trace $\operatorname{Str}(e^{-tP})$ cancel. At $\lambda=0$, the eigenspaces are $\ker D_V^+$ and $\ker D_V^-$; their signed dimension difference is the Fredholm index from [F3]. The diagonal kernel series is uniformly convergent, so integrating its pointwise supertrace equals the sum of these eigenspace traces. This proves the stated identity for every $t>0$.

If $M$ is empty all Hilbert spaces and integrals are zero. In dimension zero the spectrum is the finite-dimensional zero operator and the same identity is direct; the analytic estimates above are only invoked in positive even dimension. The trace equality was obtained from the explicit smooth kernel series, not from an unproved diagonal trace theorem.

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold of even dimension $2m$, and let $V=V^+\oplus V^-$ be a finite-rank smooth complex vector bundle with a Hermitian metric linear in its first variable. Write $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathbb C}(T^*M,-g)$ for the complex Clifford bundle generated by cotangent vectors with relation $\xi\eta+\eta\xi=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)$. A **graded Hermitian Clifford action** is a smooth real-linear map $c:T^*M\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ such that $c(\xi)^*=-c(\xi)$, $c(\xi)V^\pm\subseteq V^\mp$, and $c(\xi)c(\eta)+c(\eta)c(\xi)=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)I$. It extends complex-linearly to the complex Clifford bundle.

A **graded Hermitian Clifford connection** is a unitary connection $\nabla^V$ preserving $V^\pm$ and satisfying
$$\nabla^V_X(c(\xi)v)=c(\nabla^{LC}_X\xi)v+c(\xi)\nabla^V_Xv$$
for smooth $X,\xi,v$, where $\nabla^{LC}$ is the Levi–Civita connection. In a local orthonormal coframe $(e^i)$ define
$$D_Vv=\sum_i c(e^i)\nabla^V_{e_i}v.$$
The operator is odd, so its chiral part is $D_V^+:C^\infty(V^+)\to C^\infty(V^-)$. The formula's frame independence, formal symmetry on closed $M$, and global bundle well-definedness are proved in [[lem-geometric-dirac-operator-is-well-defined]]. A domain and index are assigned only under the compact hypotheses of later items.

Use the complex PA-04 Clifford classification in [A1] and [A2]. For the complexification of a positive-definite real $n$-space, the irreducible Clifford spinor modules and their restrictions to full-even Spin are as follows:

- If $n=2m$ with $m\ge1$, the unique irreducible complex Clifford module has dimension $2^m$; its restriction to Spin is $S^+\oplus S^-$, with two inequivalent irreducible half-spin modules of dimension $2^{m-1}$ each.
- If $n=2m+1$, there are two inequivalent irreducible complex Clifford modules, each of dimension $2^m$; their restrictions to Spin are isomorphic to the same irreducible complex Spin module of dimension $2^m$.
- For $n=0$, there is one one-dimensional complex Clifford spinor; for $n=1$, there are two one-dimensional Clifford spinors and their restrictions to $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ agree.

Separately, assuming AC, every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of the compact Hausdorff group $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is completely reducible. This applies to all finite-dimensional continuous representations, not only the spinor modules above.

Use the plus-square convention $v^2=Q(v)1$. For the real standard form $Q_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^2-\sum_{j=1}^q x_{p+j}^2$, write $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0$ for the even part of the canonical $\mathbb Z/2$ grading. If $p>0$, then

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. For the standard complex form $Q_n(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$ with $n>0$, the even subalgebra is isomorphic over $\mathbb C$ to $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n-1}(\mathbb C)$, the complex Clifford algebra on $n-1$ generators each having square $-1$, and hence to the standard complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.

Let $n=p+q$, let $r$ be the residue of $p-q$ modulo $8$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and use $v^2=Q(v)1$ with signature ordered $(+^p,-^q)$. For every nondegenerate real form of signature $(p,q)$, the real Clifford algebra is

| $r$ | parity of $n$ | $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}$ |
|---:|:---:|---|
| $0$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $1$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

derivations.claim: The positive generators satisfy $c_+(v)^2=|v|^2$, so $c_0(v)^2=-|v|^2$ and their polarized relation is the required negative one. Spin equivariance is preserved: $\sigma(h)c_0(v)\sigma(h)^{-1}=i\,c_+(\rho(h)v)=c_0(\rho(h)v)$. Its negative-sign volume chirality is $i^m\prod_j(i c_+(e^j))=(-1)^m i^m\prod_jc_+(e^j)$, so the two half-spin labels are exchanged when $m$ is odd, with dimensions unchanged. Reversing the order of the $n$ pairwise anticommuting generators takes $n(n-1)/2=m(2m-1)$ swaps, and their squares contribute $(-1)^n=1$. Hence $(c_1\cdots c_n)^2=(-1)^m$. Since $(i^m)^2=(-1)^m$, $\Gamma^2=1$. For any $k$, moving $c_k$ through the other $n-1$ factors changes the sign by $(-1)^{n-1}=-1$; thus $\Gamma c_k=-c_k\Gamma$, and linearity gives the same relation for every covector.

The product $c_1\cdots c_n$ is fully alternating because distinct orthonormal generators anticommute. Under an oriented orthogonal basis change $A\in SO(n)$, its top exterior coefficient is multiplied by $\det A=1$, so $\Gamma$ is independent of the chosen oriented orthonormal basis. Since $\Gamma^2=1$ over $\mathbb C$, the projections $(I\pm\Gamma)/2$ split $S_0=S_0^+\oplus S_0^-$. Anticommutation shows each $c_0(\xi)$ exchanges the two eigenspaces. Their dimensions are equal to $2^{m-1}$ by [F2]. The exact full and even matrix factors are those in [A1].

citations.quote: Equip $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ with its finite-dimensional real topology, Pin and full-even Spin with the subspace topology, and $O(V,B)$ and $SO(V,B)$ with their matrix topologies. The maps in [[thm-real-pin-spin-image-kernel-and-compactness]] are continuous central two-sheeted covering maps. This is a topological assertion in addition to the algebraic exactness of those sequences.

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space with $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ use $v^2=Q(v)1$. Use the grading involution $\alpha$ and Clifford conjugation $\bar x$ from [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Let $\mathrm{Cl}^0$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^1$ be the even and odd parts for word-length parity. Define the **unrestricted twisted Clifford normalizer** as the set

$$\Gamma(V,B)=\{x\in\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times:\alpha(x)v x^{-1}\in V\text{ for every }v\in V\},\qquad \rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)v x^{-1}.$$

Define the normalized anisotropic vectors $U(V,Q)=\{u\in V:|Q(u)|=1\}$. For $\dim V>0$, **Pin$(V,Q)$** is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times$ generated by $U(V,Q)$; for $V=0$, set Pin$(0)=\{1,-1\}$. Define

$$\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)=\operatorname{Pin}(V,Q)\cap\mathrm{Cl}^0,\qquad \operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)=\{x\in\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q):N(x)=1\}.$$

For definite signature, the conventional names Pin$^+(n)$ and Pin$^-(n)$ mean the groups in $\mathrm{Cl}_{n,0}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$, respectively. In mixed signature the subscript “full” is retained because the full even subgroup and the norm-one subgroup can have different images.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $n\ge3$, the connected double cover $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n)\to SO(n)$ from [[thm-real-pin-spin-topological-double-covers]] has simply connected total space and is the universal covering group of $SO(n)$. The proof uses the explicit locally trivial sphere bundle

$$\operatorname{Spin}(n-1)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}(n)\xrightarrow{x\mapsto\rho_x(e_n)}S^{n-1}$$

from [[lem-euclidean-spin-sphere-bundle-local-sections]]. No universal-cover assertion is made for $n=1$ or $n=2$.

Assume AC. Let $f:B'\to B$ be a continuous map of paracompact Hausdorff CGWH bases of CW homotopy type and let
$E\to B$ be a numerable real bundle of rank $n\geq0$. Then
$$w_i(f^*E)=f^*w_i(E)\quad\text{for every }i\geq0,\qquad w(f^*E)=f^*w(E).$$
Consequently the Stiefel–Whitney classes depend only on the isomorphism class
of the bundle.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ and $F\to B$ be numerable real vector bundles of ranks
$m,n\geq0$ over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type. Then the total Stiefel–Whitney classes
satisfy
$$w(E\oplus F)=w(E)w(F),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad w_k(E\oplus F)=\sum_{i+j=k}w_i(E)w_j(F)\quad(k\geq0).$$
In particular $w(0_B)=1$, and adjoining a trivial summand does not change the
positive classes: $w(E\oplus\varepsilon_B^r)=w(E)$ for $r\geq0$.

Assume AC, let $E\to B$ be a numerable real vector bundle of rank $n\geq1$ over
a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type (an admissible base on
this page), and let
$x_E\in H^1(P(E);\mathbb F_2)$ be its tautological degree-one class. By
[[thm-mod-two-real-projective-bundle-theorem]] there are unique classes
$c_i\in H^i(B;\mathbb F_2)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, with
$$x_E^n+c_1x_E^{n-1}+\cdots+c_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^n(P(E);\mathbb F_2).$$
The **Stiefel–Whitney classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$w_i(E):=c_i\in H^i(B;\mathbb F_2)\quad(1\leq i\leq n).$$
The definition is completed by the conventions $w_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb F_2)$
and $w_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Stiefel–Whitney class** is the
finite sum
$$w(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}w_i(E)=1+w_1(E)+\cdots+w_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb F_2).$$
For the zero bundle of rank $0$ the conventions give $w(0_B)=1$.

Applying the definition to a line bundle $L\to B$: here $n=1$,
$P(L)\cong B$ over $B$ and $\gamma_L\cong L$ under that identification, so the
relation is $x_L+w_1(L)=0$, that is, $w_1(L)=x_L$, and
$w(L)=1+x_L$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle over a
path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex and let $\rho_2$ denote reduction
of coefficients modulo two. Then
$$w_{2i+1}(E_{\mathbb R})=0,\qquad w_{2i}(E_{\mathbb R})=\rho_2c_i(E) \qquad(i\geq0),$$
where $w$ denotes the total Stiefel-Whitney class of the underlying real
bundle.

Assume AC. Identify $\mathbb{CP}^\infty=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^\infty)$,
the space of complex lines in $\mathbb C^\infty$, and let
$u=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ be the class of
the tautological complex line. Then
$$H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\cdot u^k,\qquad H^{2k+1}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=0\qquad(k\geq0),$$
so $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[u]$ is a polynomial ring; and
$H_k(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one for even $k$ and zero
for odd $k$, in particular finitely generated in every degree.

Assume AC. For a path-connected CW complex $X$ with a vertex basepoint, the
first Chern class induces a natural group isomorphism
$$c_1:\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H^2(X;\mathbb Z),$$
where $\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)$ is the group of isomorphism
classes of numerable complex line bundles under tensor product. The same
statement holds for a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CGWH space of CW
homotopy type.

Assume AC. For a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base $X$ and $n\geq0$,
pullback of $\gamma_n^+$ gives a natural bijection

$$[X,\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^\infty)]=[X,B\operatorname{SO}(n)]\cong\operatorname{Vect}^{\mathbb R,+}_n(X),$$

where the right side consists of orientation-preserving isomorphism classes
of numerable oriented rank-$n$ real bundles. For $n=0$ both sets are
singletons.

For $0\leq n\leq N$, the **oriented Grassmannian** is

$$\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^N)=V_n(\mathbb R^N)/\operatorname{SO}(n).$$

An ordered orthonormal frame determines its span together with the orientation
it transports from $\mathbb R^n$, and the $\operatorname{SO}(n)$ quotient
identifies exactly the frames inducing the same oriented plane. The associated
standard bundle is the tautological bundle
$\gamma_n^{+,N}$; its fiber over $(W,o)$ is $W$ with orientation $o$, in
the sense of [[def-oriented-real-vector-bundle-and-oriented-frame-bundle]].

The stable coordinate inclusions from
[[def-stiefel-space-grassmannian-and-tautological-bundle]] define

$$\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^N),$$

with the weak direct-limit topology. This chosen model is denoted
$B\operatorname{SO}(n)$.

For $n\geq1$, forgetting the orientation is the double cover
$\operatorname{Gr}_n^+\to\operatorname{Gr}_n$, since a positive-dimensional
real vector space has exactly two orientations. After forgetting orientation,
$\gamma_n^+$ is the pullback of $\gamma_n$ along this cover. For $n=0$, both
Grassmannians are points and the tautological bundle has its canonical
rank-zero orientation.

For a numerable rank-$n$ real vector bundle with a supplied bundle metric,
orientations are naturally in bijection with reductions of its orthonormal
frame bundle from $\operatorname O(n)$ to $\operatorname{SO}(n)$.
Orientation-preserving isometries preserve these reductions.

Assume AC, inherited from the cited bundle, cohomology, or operation suppliers. For n≥1, the forgetful map Gr⁺_n(R∞)=BSO(n)→Gr_n(R∞)=BO(n) is a two-sheeted cover, including n=1, where it is S∞→RP∞. Each Schubert cell has exactly two lifted cells, and these cells give BSO(n) the CW weak topology with finite boundary support. Set BSO(0) to the point.

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $0\leq n\leq N$.
The **Stiefel space**

$$V_n(\mathbb F^N)=\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n):\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\}$$

has the subspace topology from $(\mathbb F^N)^n$. The group
$K_n=\operatorname O(n)$ in the real case and
$K_n=\operatorname U(n)$ in the complex case acts freely on the right by
change of orthonormal frame. The **Grassmannian**
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)=V_n(\mathbb F^N)/K_n$ is the space of
$n$-planes with this quotient topology.

Graph charts about a plane identify nearby planes with linear maps to its
orthogonal complement. They locally trivialize
$V_n(\mathbb F^N)\to\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$ as a principal
$K_n$-bundle. Its associated standard vector bundle, in the convention of
[[def-frame-bundle-and-associated-vector-bundle]], is the **tautological
bundle**

$$\gamma_n^N=\{(W,v)\in\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)\times\mathbb F^N:v\in W\}.$$

Equivalently, its graph-chart transition matrices glue it by
[[thm-vector-bundles-glued-from-transition-cocycles]].

The coordinate inclusions $\mathbb F^N\subseteq\mathbb F^{N+1}$ define
compatible inclusions of Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and tautological
bundles. Write

$$V_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}V_n(\mathbb F^N),\qquad \operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^\infty)=\bigcup_{N\geq n}\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N),$$

with the weak direct-limit topology: a set is closed exactly when its
intersection with every finite stage is closed. The later Schubert theorem
identifies this with the weak topology in
[[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]. For $n=0$,
the Stiefel spaces, Grassmannians, and their stable colimits are points, and
$\gamma_0$ is the zero bundle.

For $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and fixed $n\geq0$, the stable
Stiefel space $V_n(\mathbb F^\infty)$ is contractible. For $n=0$ it is
already a point. For $n>0$ there is an explicit contraction that first moves
every frame to odd coordinates and then rotates it to a fixed frame in the
even coordinates. The odd- and even-coordinate embeddings are each homotopic
to the identity through the same Gram-normalized injective linear paths.
Every compact topological space is paracompact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Every open cover
of a paracompact Hausdorff space admits a locally finite partition of unity
subordinate to it.

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

Let $n\ge2$ and assume the Axiom of Choice. If a CW complex $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected, then for every $x\in X$
$$\widetilde H_i(X;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(0\le i<n),\qquad h:\pi_n(X,x)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_n(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The same conclusion holds for an $(n-1)$-connected space already known to be homotopy equivalent to a CW complex, using an actual homotopy equivalence.

Separately, for $n=1$ and any nonempty path-connected space $X$, the map $h:\pi_1(X,x)\to H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the abelianization map: it is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup, and $\widetilde H_0(X;\mathbb Z)=0$. This degree-one assertion is choice-free and requires no CW-type assumption. A bare weak CW approximation is not the hypothesis used for the CW-type transfer above.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.

For a rank-$n$ real vector bundle $\xi\to X$, form the **orientation cover**
$\operatorname{Or}(\xi)\to X$ whose fiber is the set of orientations of
$\xi_x$. In a linear chart, an orientation is the standard orientation or its
negative, and a transition matrix acts by the sign of its determinant. These
charts give a two-sheeted cover when $n\geq1$.

An **orientation** of $\xi$ is a section of this cover, equivalently a
continuous fiberwise choice of orientation. The zero vector space has its
canonical orientation, so a rank-zero bundle has one orientation rather than
two. A fiberwise invertible bundle map between oriented bundles is
**orientation-preserving** when it carries the selected orientation to the
selected orientation; in oriented local frames its matrices have positive
determinant.

The **oriented frame bundle**
$\operatorname{Fr}^+(\xi)\subseteq\operatorname{Fr}(\xi)$ consists of frames
that transport the standard orientation of $\mathbb R^n$ to the selected
orientation of $\xi_x$. Oriented linear charts identify it with
$U\times\operatorname{GL}_n^+(\mathbb R)$, and precomposition makes it a
principal $\operatorname{GL}_n^+(\mathbb R)$-bundle. This construction uses
neither a metric nor a choice principle; a metric-dependent
$\operatorname{SO}(n)$ reduction is treated separately.

For a subgroup $H\subseteq G$, an **$H$-reduction** of a principal
$G$-bundle $P$ is a principal $H$-subbundle $Q\subseteq P$ for which
$Q\times_HG\to P$, $[q,g]\mapsto qg$, is an isomorphism of the principal
bundles defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold with a Riemannian metric, and let $\mathcal U=\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover whose members are strongly geodesically convex in the convention of [[thm-existence-of-geodesically-convex-neighborhoods]]. Let $N(\mathcal U)$ be the abstract simplicial complex whose finite nonempty subsets $\sigma\subset I$ are simplices exactly when $U_\sigma:=\bigcap_{i\in\sigma}U_i$ is nonempty. Then the geometric realization $|N(\mathcal U)|$ is homotopy equivalent to $M$. Writing $H^*_{\mathrm{simp}}(N;\mathbb F_2)$ for the cohomology of the simplicial cochain complex, the natural comparison identifies it with $H^*(M;\mathbb F_2)$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume the choice principles carried by the cited topology results:
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the Lindelof step and the Axiom of Choice for the
metrization corollary. Then every topological manifold is regular, metrizable,
and paracompact.

A space $X$ is **weak Hausdorff** (WH) if every continuous map $u:K\to X$ from a compact Hausdorff space has closed image. Here compactness and Hausdorffness are separate requirements.

A subset $F\subseteq X$ is **k-closed** if $u^{-1}(F)$ is closed for every such test $u$. The space $kX$ has the same underlying set as $X$ and these closed sets. A space is **compactly generated** (CG) if $kX=X$, and **CGWH** if it is both CG and WH. The topology and mapping properties are established in the following lemmas.

For CG spaces put $X\times_k Y=k(X\times Y)$. Let $C_0(Y,Z)$ be the continuous maps with subbasic opens
$$W(u,K,O)=\{f:Y\to Z\text{ continuous}:f(u(K))\subseteq O\},$$
where $K$ is compact Hausdorff, $u:K\to Y$ is continuous, and $O$ is open in $Z$. Put $C(Y,Z)=kC_0(Y,Z)$. For based spaces, $C_*(Y,Z)$ is the kification of the subspace of basepoint-preserving maps. Put $\Omega Z=C_*((I,\{0,1\}),(Z,z_0))$, meaning the kified subspace of maps whose two endpoint values are $z_0$.

Categorical products and based constructions below use CGWH spaces unless explicitly stated otherwise. Cubical homotopy classes are still defined for arbitrary topological spaces. Homotopies relative to a subspace have the meaning of [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]. For WH domains the test-image mapping topology equals the compact-Hausdorff-subspace convention; no analogous identification with arbitrary compact subsets is asserted here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Each nonempty finite intersection of the good cover is contractible by [F6], so the covering in [F1] lifts each $g_{ij}$ to a continuous $\widetilde g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to\operatorname{Spin}_{\rm full}(n)$. Full AC supplies this family of lifts and signs. Choose $\widetilde g_{ji}=\widetilde g_{ij}^{-1}$ and $\widetilde g_{ii}=1$. Since $\rho(\widetilde g_{ij}\widetilde g_{jk}\widetilde g_{ki})=1$, the triple product is a locally constant central sign $\epsilon_{ijk}\in\{\pm1\}$.

Associativity and centrality give $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ikl}=\epsilon_{jkl}\epsilon_{ijl}$ on every nonempty quadruple intersection: substitute the four chosen lifts, cancel each shared lift with its inverse, and commute only the resulting central signs. Thus $\epsilon$ is a degree-two cocycle on the cover nerve. If the lifts are changed by signs $a_{ij}=a_{ji}^{-1}$, the triple product changes by the Čech coboundary $\delta a$; hence its cohomology class $\eta(E)$ is independent of these choices. By [F7], the cover nerve computes singular cohomology of $M$, so $\eta(E)$ is a well-defined element of $H^2(M;\mathbb F_2)$, natural under pullback and refinement.

If $\eta(E)=0$, choose signs $a_{ij}$ with $\epsilon=\delta a$ and replace $\widetilde g_{ij}$ by $a_{ij}\widetilde g_{ij}$, using additive $\mathbb F_2$ notation for the signs. The new triple products are $1$, so these transitions glue a principal Spin bundle and the maps $\rho(\widetilde g_{ij})=g_{ij}$ glue its equivariant map to $P_{SO}(E)$. Conversely, transitions of any Spin lift have triple product $1$, so relative to the chosen lifts their signs make $\epsilon$ a coboundary. Thus a lift exists exactly when $\eta(E)=0$.

For $n\ge3$, [F5] gives a CW model $BSO(n)=\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^\infty)$ and its contractible stable Stiefel total space. Its tautological frame map is locally trivial: graph charts give continuous oriented orthonormal frames by Gram–Schmidt, with transition maps in $SO(n)$. This principal bundle is a Serre fibration: for each disk lifting problem, pull back along its homotopy over $D^k\times[0,1]$; this compact Hausdorff parameter space is paracompact, so the pullback is numerable by [F5] and is a Hurewicz fibration. Its long exact sequence, contractibility of the total space, connectedness of $SO(n)$, and the universal double cover [F2] give $\pi_1(BSO(n))=0$ and $\pi_2(BSO(n))\cong\pi_1(SO(n))\cong\mathbb Z/2$. The stable Stiefel space is nonempty and contractible and maps onto $BSO(n)$, so $BSO(n)$ is path-connected. The first Hurewicz theorem and UCT [F5] therefore give $H^2(BSO(n);\mathbb F_2)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z/2,\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2$. The 1-skeleton is a graph. Its bundle is trivial over each closed edge, since the interval is paracompact and contractible and the oriented-bundle classifier in [F5] classifies it by a map $[0,1]\to BSO(n)$, necessarily homotopic to a constant map. Choose a point in each vertex fiber and, using full AC, an edge section for each edge. Because $SO(n)$ is path-connected, modify each edge section by a group path so that its endpoints are the chosen vertex points. These sections glue continuously by the weak topology on the 1-skeleton, so the universal frame bundle is trivial there. For each oriented 2-cell, trivialize the pulled-back bundle over its characteristic disk and record whether the boundary frame loop in $SO(n)$ lifts to a closed loop in Spin. This defines a cellular obstruction 2-cochain. For a 3-cell, the bundle pulled back to its characteristic disk is trivial and therefore has a Spin lift; restricting that lift to the boundary sphere makes the obstruction evaluate to zero on the cellular attaching 2-cycle. By the cellular coboundary formula, this mod-two sum of 2-cell obstruction values is the coboundary evaluated on that 3-cell, so the obstruction cochain is a cocycle. Changing the chosen lift on a 1-cell changes its boundary signs by the cellular coboundary of that 1-cochain. Changing local frame sections by $h_i:U_i\to SO(n)$ has the same effect: each $h_i$ lifts on the contractible $U_i$, and the lifted transition defects change by the coboundary of those local signs. Thus the class is independent of the trivializations. On each 2-simplex of the good-cover nerve, the boundary loop is the triple transition product from step 1.1, so its endpoint sign is exactly $\epsilon_{ijk}$. Naturality under pullback and the nerve comparison [F7] identify the pullback of this universal obstruction class with $\eta(E)$.

If a lift exists, any other lifted cocycle differs from it by a sign-valued degree-one cochain $b_{ij}$. Both are cocycles, so $\delta b=0$. An isomorphism over the fixed $SO$ bundle is given locally by signs $b_i$; it changes the difference cocycle by $\delta(b_i)$. Therefore isomorphism classes of lifts are a free transitive $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$-set. The action is twisting by the associated principal $\{\pm1\}$-bundle; freeness follows because a twisting cocycle that is a coboundary is removed by that local sign isomorphism, and transitivity follows from the cocycle difference.

For $n\ge3$, the clutching loop that rotates an oriented two-plane through $2\pi$ and is the identity on its orthogonal complement represents the generator of $\pi_1SO(n)$, hence corresponds under the fibration boundary isomorphism in step 3.2 to a generator of $\pi_2BSO(n)$. Its Spin lift is $t\mapsto\cos(\pi t)+e_1e_2\sin(\pi t)$, which starts at $1$ and ends at $-1$, so the universal obstruction evaluates to $1$. The associated oriented plane bundle over $S^2$ is the underlying real Hopf line, whose $c_1$ is a generator; [F4] makes its $w_2$ the nonzero reduction. Adding a trivial $(n-2)$-plane preserves $w_2$ by [F3]. Hence $w_2$ and $\eta$ are both the unique nonzero element of $H^2(BSO(n);\mathbb F_2)$ computed in step 3.2, and are equal.

For $n=2$, $SO(2)\cong S^1$ and direct Clifford multiplication gives $\operatorname{Spin}(2)\cong S^1$ with $z\mapsto z^2$. Thus $BSO(2)\simeq\mathbb{CP}^\infty$, $H^2(BSO(2);\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2$, and the degree-one clutching loop again fails to lift closed. Its universal oriented plane is the realification of the Hopf line; [F4] gives $w_2=\rho_2c_1$, which evaluates to $1$ on that generator. The two classes are again equal. For $n=1$, the oriented orthonormal frame bundle has structure group $SO(1)=1$ and $w_2(E)=0$ by rank; its lifts are principal $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ bundles, whose sign transitions modulo sign-valued vertex changes are exactly $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$.

By [F8], $P_{SO}(E)$ is numerable; [F9] verifies the paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base hypotheses of the oriented-bundle classifier in [F5], which supplies an oriented bundle isomorphism from $E$ to the pullback of the tautological bundle. The positive square-root metric correction in [F5] identifies their $SO(n)$ frame bundles, giving a classifying map $f:M\to BSO(n)$ for the actual $P_{SO}(E)$. Naturality of the local lifting obstruction and of $w_2$, together with the nerve comparison [F7], pulls the universal equality $\eta=w_2$ back to $\eta(E)=w_2(E)$. Step 3.1 proves existence iff this class vanishes, and step 4.1 proves the torsor statement. The empty-base case has one empty lift and $H^1=0$; rank zero lies outside this item's stated rank range; no claim that the repo's Spin(0) convention lacks a sign-bundle torsor is made. The only nonempty choices are the local lifts in step 1.1 and the cochain primitive in step 3.1, both covered by full AC [A1].

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$. For $n\ge1$, put $\mathbb R^n:=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb R$ with its
usual topology; for $n=0$ put $\mathbb R^0:=\{0\}$, the one-point space. A
**topological $n$-manifold without boundary** (or briefly an **$n$-manifold**) is
a topological space $M$ satisfying:

1. $M$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]);
2. $M$ is second countable ([[def-second-countable-space]]);
3. $M$ is **locally Euclidean of dimension $n$**: every $p\in M$ has an open
   neighbourhood $U\subseteq M$ homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

The empty space satisfies all three conditions vacuously, so $M=\varnothing$ is
an $n$-manifold for every $n$; this degenerate instance is kept, and statements
about nonempty manifolds name the hypothesis. In dimension zero, condition 3
forces the one-point neighbourhoods of points to be open singletons, so a
$0$-manifold is exactly a discrete second-countable space with at most countably
many points.

Use the complex PA-04 Clifford classification in [A1] and [A2]. For the complexification of a positive-definite real $n$-space, the irreducible Clifford spinor modules and their restrictions to full-even Spin are as follows:

- If $n=2m$ with $m\ge1$, the unique irreducible complex Clifford module has dimension $2^m$; its restriction to Spin is $S^+\oplus S^-$, with two inequivalent irreducible half-spin modules of dimension $2^{m-1}$ each.
- If $n=2m+1$, there are two inequivalent irreducible complex Clifford modules, each of dimension $2^m$; their restrictions to Spin are isomorphic to the same irreducible complex Spin module of dimension $2^m$.
- For $n=0$, there is one one-dimensional complex Clifford spinor; for $n=1$, there are two one-dimensional Clifford spinors and their restrictions to $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ agree.

Separately, assuming AC, every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of the compact Hausdorff group $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is completely reducible. This applies to all finite-dimensional continuous representations, not only the spinor modules above.

Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $H$-bundle, meaning that the
topological principal charts of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]] are diffeomorphisms, and
let $\rho:H\to GL(V)$ be a smooth finite-dimensional real representation.
Define a right action on $P\times V$ by

$$(p,v)\cdot h=(ph,\rho(h)^{-1}v).$$

The **vector bundle associated to $P$ and $\rho$** is the quotient set with
quotient topology

$$P\times_HV=(P\times V)/H.$$

Write $[p,v]$ for the orbit of $(p,v)$. Equivalently, the generating relation
is

$$[ph,v]=[p,\rho(h)v].$$

The projection is

$$r:P\times_HV\to M,\qquad r([p,v])=\pi(p).$$

It is well defined because $\pi(ph)=\pi(p)$ and continuous by the quotient
universal property [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The inverse in the
diagonal action is essential: it makes the displayed relation and the right
action law agree. The quotient construction itself uses no choices. The
homogeneous principal bundle of
[[thm-g-to-g-mod-h-is-a-smooth-principal-h-bundle]] is one instance, not a
hypothesis of the general definition. The next theorem supplies the smooth
vector-bundle atlas in the sense of
[[def-vector-bundle-chart-and-transition-function]].

Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $H$-bundle and let
$\rho:H\to GL(V)$ be a smooth representation on a finite-dimensional real
vector space. Then $P\times_HV$ has a unique smooth rank-$\dim V$ vector-bundle
structure over $M$ whose local trivializations are induced by principal-bundle
sections. If $s_i=s_jg_{ji}$ on an overlap, the transition from the
$i$-coordinates to the $j$-coordinates is $\rho(g_{ji})$.
Every supplied smooth Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary, has exactly one Levi–Civita connection. The construction adds no choice assumption.

If $e'=eA$ are two frames on an overlap, their matrices for the same connection satisfy
$$\omega'=A^{-1}\omega A+A^{-1}dA.$$
All entries of $dA$ are differentials of scalar functions; the order of the matrix factors is as displayed.

Let a smooth vector bundle be covered by supplied frames $e_\alpha$ on $U_\alpha$, with $e_\beta=e_\alpha A_{\alpha\beta}$ on overlaps. Matrices of smooth one-forms $\omega_\alpha$ are the local matrices of a unique connection if and only if
$$\omega_\beta=A_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}\omega_\alpha A_{\alpha\beta}+A_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dA_{\alpha\beta}$$
on every overlap. No local finiteness or choice assumption is required for this gluing statement.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on $M$ in
the sense of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], and let $X,Y,Z$ be
smooth vector fields. With the sign convention used throughout this page, the
**curvature of $\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$

where $[X,Y]$ is the bracket of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. We usually write $R$ when the
connection is understood. The connection is **flat** or **curvature-free** when
$R(X,Y)Z=0$ for every triple of smooth vector fields.

The bracket correction is part of the definition. The raw commutator of two
covariant derivatives is not function-linear in its differentiating fields.
No metric or torsion hypothesis is imposed here. On an empty or
zero-dimensional manifold the condition is vacuous; on manifolds with boundary
the same formula uses the ambient tangent bundle supplied by the definition of
an affine connection.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold
it gives the unique zero four-tensor; in dimension one the same formula applies
and later symmetries force it to vanish. It is valid up to the boundary when a
Riemannian manifold with boundary is supplied.

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

Use the plus-square convention $v^2=Q(v)1$. For the real standard form $Q_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^2-\sum_{j=1}^q x_{p+j}^2$, write $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0$ for the even part of the canonical $\mathbb Z/2$ grading. If $p>0$, then

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. For the standard complex form $Q_n(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$ with $n>0$, the even subalgebra is isomorphic over $\mathbb C$ to $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n-1}(\mathbb C)$, the complex Clifford algebra on $n-1$ generators each having square $-1$, and hence to the standard complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.

Let $n=p+q$, let $r$ be the residue of $p-q$ modulo $8$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and use $v^2=Q(v)1$ with signature ordered $(+^p,-^q)$. For every nondegenerate real form of signature $(p,q)$, the real Clifford algebra is

| $r$ | parity of $n$ | $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}$ |
|---:|:---:|---|
| $0$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $1$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, let $J=\operatorname{diag}(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n)$ be its matrix in an orthogonal anisotropic basis with $\epsilon_i=Q(e_i)\in\{1,-1\}$, and let $SO(V,B)$ have the subspace topology from matrices. There is a neighborhood $U$ of the identity in $SO(V,B)$ and a continuous map $s:U\to\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)$ with $s(I)=1$ and $\rho(s(A))=A$.

derivations.claim: By [F0], $M$ has a countable base. From the supplied local trivializing cover of the topological Spin lift, choose for each basis element contained in some trivializing open set one such set; these countably many sets cover $M$. Choose a local section on each. On overlaps its continuous transition $h_{ij}$ lifts the smooth oriented-frame transition $g_{ij}$. At each point, translate the local logarithm/exponential section in [F5] to a smooth inverse branch of $\rho$ near $g_{ij}(x)$. After restricting to a connected neighborhood, the continuous lift $h_{ij}$ agrees with one of the two inverse branches, so $h_{ij}$ is smooth. The resulting principal charts have smooth transitions and define a smooth structure on the actual supplied lift. This structure is Hausdorff because the base is Hausdorff and each fiber is separated in a product chart. It is second-countable because it is covered by countably many charts $U_i\times\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ and the finite-dimensional Clifford group is second-countable. The right action is smooth in these charts. Realify the smooth complex representation $\sigma: \operatorname{Spin}(n)\to GL_{\mathbb R}(S_{0,\mathbb R})$. The associated-bundle theorem [F2] now applies to this smooth, second-countable principal bundle. Multiplication by $i$ commutes with $\sigma(h_{ij})$, so it descends to a smooth endomorphism $J$ with $J^2=-I$ and the associated charts are complex-linear; the Spin-invariant chirality operator and its eigenspaces descend as well.

Start with any positive Hermitian form on $S_0$ and average it over the finite group of signed monomials in the negative-square generators $c_0(e^j)$. Each generator becomes unitary; since its square is $-I$, its adjoint is its negative. Real linearity then makes every $c_0(v)$ skew-Hermitian, and unit vectors act unitarily. The positive generators are $c_+=-ic_0$, so their unit-vector products, and hence the full-even Spin action, are unitary too. Chirality is unitary and has square one, hence is selfadjoint. Thus this one form is both Clifford-compatible and Spin-invariant, and descends to a smooth associated Hermitian metric. Averaging over Spin alone would not ensure the vector adjoint relation. Let $\omega_i$ be the local $\mathfrak{so}(n)$-valued Levi–Civita connection matrix and let $\widehat\omega_i=(d\rho)^{-1}\omega_i$ be its lift to $\mathfrak{spin}(n)$. The connection matrices $d\sigma(\widehat\omega_i)$ obey the frame-change law [F3], so they glue uniquely. In the positive-square cover, the infinitesimal lift of an orthogonal matrix $A$ is the negative Clifford bivector; substitution $c_+=-ic_0$ cancels that sign and gives the local spin action $\frac14\sum_{a,b}\langle Ae_a,e_b\rangle c_0(e^a)c_0(e^b)$. Expanding the Clifford relation gives $[c(e^a)c(e^b),c(e^k)]=2(\delta_{ak}c(e^b)-\delta_{bk}c(e^a))$, so the lifted connection intertwines the defining $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ action and Clifford multiplication. Thus the glued spin connection is unitary, preserves chirality, and is Clifford-compatible.

Locally the complex Clifford algebra in even dimension is a full matrix algebra by [F1]. Its matrix idempotents split $V$ into smooth subbundles and its matrix units identify those subbundles, giving a smooth evaluation isomorphism $V\cong S_0\widehat\otimes W$ with $W=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cl}}(S_0,V)$. The induced multiplicity grading is $\Gamma_W=(\Gamma_{S_0}\otimes I)\Gamma_V$, so $\Gamma_V=\Gamma_{S_0}\otimes\Gamma_W$. In a local factorization the difference $
abla^V-
abla^S\otimes I$ commutes with Clifford multiplication, because both connections are Clifford-compatible. The full matrix algebra has commutant $I\otimes\operatorname{End}(W)$, so this difference uniquely defines a smooth multiplicity connection $
abla^W$; it is unitary and preserves $\Gamma_W$ because both original connections are unitary and preserve their gradings. On an overlap write the change of factorization as $T_ eta=T_\alpha(\sigma(h_{\alpha eta})\otimes B_{\alpha eta})$, where $B_{\alpha eta}$ is the smooth invertible multiplicity transition. The connection transformation law [F3], after subtracting the spin-connection law, gives $\omega^W_ eta=B_{\alpha eta}^{-1}\omega^W_\alpha B_{\alpha eta}+B_{\alpha eta}^{-1}dB_{\alpha eta}$. Thus the local multiplicity connections glue. Their curvature satisfies $F^V=F^S\otimes I+I\otimes F^W$, with $F^S=c(R^{LC})$ by [F4], so $F^{V/S}=I\otimes F^W$ and is genuinely a global commutant-valued curvature.

On overlaps, $F^W_\beta=B_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}F^W_\alpha B_{\alpha\beta}$ and $\Gamma_W$ is preserved, so $\operatorname{str}_W\exp(-F^W/(2\pi i))$ is invariant and patches to a global even form. The Bianchi identity follows directly from the local connection matrix: for $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$, expansion gives $dF+\omega\wedge F-F\wedge\omega=0$. Cyclicity of supertrace then shows that the relative character is closed. For a path of compatible connections with commutant-valued difference $a_t=\dot\omega_t$, one has $\dot F_t=d^{\nabla_t}a_t$; applying Bianchi and cyclicity gives $\partial_t\operatorname{str}_W e^{\lambda F_t}=\lambda\,d\operatorname{str}_W(a_t e^{\lambda F_t})$, with $\lambda=-1/(2\pi i)$. The transgression forms also conjugate by $B_{\alpha\beta}$ on overlaps, so they patch. This supplies the relative cohomological interpretation for a fixed geometric module, including when no global spinor bundle $S$ exists. For $V=S\widehat\otimes E$ with its product connection, the spin connection contributes $c(R^{LC})$ and the twist contributes $I\otimes F^E$, so $F^{V/S}=F^E$ and the relative supertrace is the ordinary trace on the ungraded $E$.

In dimension zero, use $S_{0,x}=\mathbb C$ with $\Gamma_{S_{0,x}}=\varepsilon_xI$ from [[def-ahat-and-relative-chern-character-forms]]. The Clifford algebra is the scalar algebra, so evaluation identifies $S_{0,x}\widehat\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S_{0,x},V_x)$ with $V_x$. Its grading is $\Gamma_{W_x}=\varepsilon_x\Gamma_{V_x}$, making evaluation even. Every two-form is zero; thus both the spin and multiplicity curvatures are zero. On a discrete manifold these pointwise maps are smooth, the reference sign and the graded dimensions are locally constant, and the relative character $\varepsilon_x\operatorname{str}_{V_x}I$ patches globally. For $V=S_0\widehat\otimes E$ with $E$ even, $W=E$ is even and the character is its rank. This establishes the relative statement at every signed point without a Spin lift; all connection overlap, Bianchi and transgression equations there reduce to zero identities.

Assume full AC and the closed hypotheses of [[lem-dirac-heat-trace-and-mckeen-singer-index]]. In normal coordinates and radial parallel transport near the diagonal, let $h_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-d(x,y)^2/(4t)}$ and define $u_0,u_1,\ldots$ by the heat-transport recursion below. After a cutoff supported inside the injectivity-radius neighborhood, for every $r,b,N\ge0$ there is $J$ such that the parametrix
$$H_J(t,x,y)=\chi(x,y)h_t(x,y)\sum_{j=0}^Jt^ju_j(x,y)$$
satisfies
$$\|K_t-H_J(t)\|_{C_x^rC_y^b}\le C_{r,b,N}t^N\quad(0<t\le1).$$
Thus the local heat expansion has a uniform differentiated remainder of arbitrary order; no convergence of rescaled global kernels is assumed.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold and $V$ a graded Hermitian Clifford module with compatible connection as in [[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]]. Use $R(X,Y)=[
abla^{LC}_X,
abla^{LC}_Y]-
abla^{LC}_{[X,Y]}$ and $\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=g(R(X,Y)Z,W)$. In a local oriented orthonormal frame define
$$F^S_{ij}= rac14\sum_{a,b}\operatorname{Rm}(e_i,e_j,e_a,e_b)c(e^a)c(e^b),\qquad F^{V/S}_{ij}=F^V_{ij}-F^S_{ij}.$$
Then $F^{V/S}_{ij}$ commutes with Clifford multiplication and
$$D_V^2=(
abla^V)^*
abla^V+ rac{\operatorname{scal}_g}{4}I+\sum_{i<j}c(e^i)c(e^j)F^{V/S}_{ij}.$$
In particular $D_V^2$ is formally symmetric Laplace type with positive-frequency principal symbol $|\xi|^2I$.

Assume full AC. On an even-dimensional oriented Riemannian manifold with a supplied Spin lift, the realified associated construction in [[def-even-dimensional-spinor-bundle-chirality-and-spin-connection]] is a smooth Hermitian graded Clifford bundle with a global compatible spin connection. For any graded Hermitian Clifford module there is locally a graded factorization $V\cong S_0\widehat\otimes W$. Its local multiplicity spaces $W=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cl}}(S_0,V)$ and the relative curvature $F^{V/S}:=F^V-c(R^{LC})$ have transition laws for which $\operatorname{str}_W\exp(-F^{V/S}/(2\pi i))$ is a global even form. In the spin-twisted case $V=S\widehat\otimes E$, this relative curvature is the curvature $F^E$ of the supplied unitary connection. Since $\mathcal R$ is skew, $B$ is an even power series in $\mathcal R$, hence symmetric and commuting with $\mathcal R$; $\mathcal R B$ is skew. Direct differentiation gives $$tB'=B-B^2+\tfrac{t^2}{4}\mathcal R^2,$$ using $z\frac d{dz}(z\coth z)=z\coth z-z^2\operatorname{csch}^2z$, and $$\frac{a'}a=-\frac{\operatorname{tr}B}{2t},$$ since $\dim M=2m$.

Let $\phi=a(t)\exp(-x^TB(t)x/(4t))e^{-tF}$. For $L_i=\partial_i+(\mathcal R x)_i/4$, one has $L_i\phi=(- (Bx)_i/(2t)+ (\mathcal R x)_i/4)\phi$. Summing $L_i^2$ for $L_i=\partial_i+(\mathcal R x)_i/4$ gives $$\sum_iL_i^2\phi=\left(-\frac{\operatorname{tr}B}{2t}+\frac{x^TB^2x}{4t^2}-\frac{x^T\mathcal R^2x}{16}\right)\phi,$$ because the mixed term is $x^T\mathcal R Bx=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal R=0$. The equations in step 1.1 cancel the constant and quadratic coefficients of $(\partial_t-\sum_iL_i^2+F)\phi$, so $\phi$ solves the oscillator heat equation. As $t\downarrow0$, $B(t)\to I$, $a(t)\sim(4\pi t)^{-m}$, and the normalized Euclidean Gaussian tends to the delta distribution; this fixes the initial value.

At $x=0$ the Gaussian factor is $1$. The spinor supertrace kills every Clifford degree below $2m$ and multiplies the top term by $(-2i)^m$ from [F1]; combining this with $(4\pi)^{-m}$ contributes $(-i/(2\pi))^m$ to each product of $m$ curvature two-forms. The determinant factor is even in $\mathcal R$, so replacing each tangent-curvature symbol by $-i\Omega^{LC}/(2\pi)$ gives exactly $\widehat A$ in [F2]. The twisting factor $e^{-F}$ becomes $e^{iF/(2\pi)}=e^{-F/(2\pi i)}$ and its trace is the relative supertrace in [F2]. Their degree-$2m$ part is the asserted density.

No matrix of forms is diagonalized: the calculation is in a finite-dimensional graded-commutative algebra, and all formal series are degree-truncated. Endomorphisms on $W$ need not commute with one another; they commute with the scalar tangent-curvature matrix, which is all the Gaussian calculation uses. The sign is fixed by the positive-frequency symbol $ic(\xi)$ and the curvature convention in [F2]. The local spinor factor is the actual interface in [A1].

If $m=0$, the determinant of the empty matrix and the empty Gaussian factor are $1$, and all curvature two-forms vanish. Thus the displayed kernel is $I_V$, the normalized heat solution on a point as in [F1]. Its diagonal supertrace with respect to the unsigned counting density is $\operatorname{str}_V I$. Multiplying by the oriented volume form in [F3] gives the degree-zero form $\varepsilon_y\operatorname{str}_V I$. By [F2] and the reference grading, $\operatorname{str}_{W_y}I=\varepsilon_y\operatorname{str}_{V_y}I$, so this oriented form is exactly $[\widehat A\operatorname{ch}(V/S)]_0$. This distinguishes the heat density from the differential form at a negatively oriented point.
