Assume full AC. Let $M$ be closed, Riemannian, and of even dimension $n\ge2$. Let $D_V$ be the formally symmetric geometric Dirac operator of [[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]], and let $P=D_V^2$ have the Lichnerowicz form of [[lem-lichnerowicz-formula-for-geometric-dirac-operators]]. Then
$$\operatorname{dom}(\overline D_V)=H^1(M,V)=\{u\in L^2: D_Vu\in L^2\text{ distributionally}\},$$
its graph norm is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm, smooth sections are a core, and $\overline D_V$ is selfadjoint.

Assume full AC and the closed hypotheses of [[lem-dirac-maximal-domain-is-h1]]. The chiral operator
$$D_V^+:H^1(V^+)\longrightarrow L^2(V^-)$$
is Fredholm. Its kernel is $\ker D_V\cap L^2(V^+)$, its cokernel is canonically $\ker D_V\cap L^2(V^-)$, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_V^+=\dim\ker D_V^+-\dim\ker D_V^-.$$
Both kernels are finite-dimensional and consist of smooth sections.

Assume full AC. For a closed even-dimensional manifold and a graded Hermitian geometric Clifford module, let $P=D_V^2$ with the $H^2$ selfadjoint domain. Its spectrum is discrete, nonnegative, of finite multiplicities, and has smooth eigensections. For $t>0$, $e^{-tP}$ is trace class and has a smooth kernel $K_t(x,y)$. The diagonal series and its derivatives converge uniformly for each $t>0$, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_V^+=\operatorname{Str}(e^{-tP})=\int_M\operatorname{str}K_t(x,x)\,d\operatorname{vol}_g(x),\qquad t>0.$$

Assume full AC and the closed hypotheses of [[lem-dirac-heat-trace-and-mckeen-singer-index]]. In normal coordinates and radial parallel transport near the diagonal, let $h_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-d(x,y)^2/(4t)}$ and define $u_0,u_1,\ldots$ by the heat-transport recursion below. After a cutoff supported inside the injectivity-radius neighborhood, for every $r,b,N\ge0$ there is $J$ such that the parametrix
$$H_J(t,x,y)=\chi(x,y)h_t(x,y)\sum_{j=0}^Jt^ju_j(x,y)$$
satisfies
$$\|K_t-H_J(t)\|_{C_x^rC_y^b}\le C_{r,b,N}t^N\quad(0<t\le1).$$
Thus the local heat expansion has a uniform differentiated remainder of arbitrary order; no convergence of rescaled global kernels is assumed.

Assume full AC. Near any point $y$ of a closed even-dimensional geometric Clifford module, choose normal coordinates and radial parallel transport. Give $\partial_i$, $c(e^i)$, and $x^i$ Getzler degrees $1,1,-1$, respectively. The transport coefficients of [[lem-dirac-heat-parametrix-has-graph-norm-remainder]] have Getzler degree at most $2j$, and the leading operator of $D^2$ is the formal oscillator
$$P_0=-\sum_i\left(\partial_i+\frac14\sum_j\mathcal R_{ij}x^j\right)^2+F^{V/S}_y,$$
where $\mathcal R_{ij}=2F^S_{ji}(y)$ is the skew tangent-curvature matrix written in exterior-form symbols and $F^{V/S}$ is the relative twisting curvature. The diagonal supertrace coefficients vanish for $j<m$ when $n=2m$, and the $j=m$ coefficient is determined by the oscillator heat equation. For $m=0$, use the orientation-graded reference line from [[def-ahat-and-relative-chern-character-forms]]; then $P_0=0$, $u_0=I_V$, $u_j=0$ for $j>0$, and $\operatorname{str}_V u_0=\varepsilon_y\operatorname{str}_{W_y}I$.

Assume full AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-getzler-radial-gauge-oscillator-leading-term]]. In the finite-dimensional even exterior-form algebra at $y$, the heat equation for $P_0$ has the normalized Gaussian solution
$$k_t(x,0)=(4\pi t)^{-m}\det^{1/2}\!\left(\frac{t\mathcal R/2}{\sinh(t\mathcal R/2)}\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{4t}x^T\bigl((t\mathcal R/2)\coth(t\mathcal R/2)\bigr)x\right)e^{-tF^{V/S}}.$$
The square root is the formal branch with constant term $1$. Its degree-$2m$ diagonal supertrace coefficient, interpreted as an oriented top form using [[def-riemannian-volume-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and the curvature convention of [[def-ahat-and-relative-chern-character-forms]], is exactly $[\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})\operatorname{ch}(V/S)]_{2m}$.

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold of dimension $2m$ and let $\Omega^{LC}$ be the skew-symmetric matrix of curvature two-forms of the Levi–Civita connection, with curvature convention
$R(X,Y)=[\nabla_X,\nabla_Y]-\nabla_{[X,Y]}$.
Define
$$\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})=\det{}^{1/2}\!\left(\frac{i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi}{\sinh(i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi)}\right).$$
The determinant and square root are formal power series in commuting even-degree differential forms; the square-root branch has constant term $1$, and terms above degree $2m$ are discarded. This is the normalization of the A-hat characteristic form in [[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]].

For $m\ge1$ and a graded Hermitian Clifford module $V$ with compatible connection, use the local multiplicity space and relative curvature from [[lem-spinor-and-clifford-associated-bundles-are-well-defined]]. Define the **relative Chern character form** by
$$
\operatorname{ch}(V/S)=\operatorname{str}_{W}\exp\!\left(-\frac{F^{V/S}}{2\pi i}\right).
$$
Here $\operatorname{str}$ is the ordinary trace if $W$ is ungraded and the even trace minus odd trace if it is graded. The cited well-definedness lemma proves this local expression patches to a global even form. For $V=S\widehat\otimes E$ with the product connection, it is $\operatorname{tr}\exp(-F^E/(2\pi i))$. The Chern–Weil supplier [[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]] identifies the resulting cohomology classes after passage to real coefficients; this definition asserts no integral torsion identity.

For $m=0$, let $\varepsilon_x\in\{1,-1\}$ be the supplied orientation sign at $x$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). The reference zero-dimensional Clifford module $S_{0,x}$ is the complex line with grading operator $\Gamma_{S_{0,x}}=\varepsilon_x I$: it is even at a positive point and odd at a negative point. The zero-dimensional Clifford algebra is $\mathbb C$, acting by scalars. Set $W_x=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S_{0,x},V_x)$ with the grading for which evaluation $S_{0,x}\widehat\otimes W_x\to V_x$ is even. Identifying a map with its value at $1$ gives $\Gamma_{W_x}=\varepsilon_x\Gamma_{V_x}$. All curvature two-forms vanish, so $\widehat A_0=1$, $F^{V/S}=0$, and
$$\operatorname{ch}(V/S)_0(x)=\operatorname{str}_{W_x}I=\varepsilon_x\bigl(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-\bigr).$$
This formula is independent of any basis of $V_x$ and leaves its arbitrary given grading unrestricted. For $V=S_0\widehat\otimes E$ with $E$ in even degree, evaluation identifies $W=E$ in even degree, so the relative character is the ordinary rank, consistently with the product formula above. This reference-line convention makes no assertion about a Spin$(0)$ lift or its isomorphism classes.

Use the complex PA-04 Clifford classification in [A1] and [A2]. For the complexification of a positive-definite real $n$-space, the irreducible Clifford spinor modules and their restrictions to full-even Spin are as follows:

- If $n=2m$ with $m\ge1$, the unique irreducible complex Clifford module has dimension $2^m$; its restriction to Spin is $S^+\oplus S^-$, with two inequivalent irreducible half-spin modules of dimension $2^{m-1}$ each.
- If $n=2m+1$, there are two inequivalent irreducible complex Clifford modules, each of dimension $2^m$; their restrictions to Spin are isomorphic to the same irreducible complex Spin module of dimension $2^m$.
- For $n=0$, there is one one-dimensional complex Clifford spinor; for $n=1$, there are two one-dimensional Clifford spinors and their restrictions to $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ agree.

Separately, assuming AC, every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of the compact Hausdorff group $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is completely reducible. This applies to all finite-dimensional continuous representations, not only the spinor modules above.

Use the plus-square convention $v^2=Q(v)1$. For the real standard form $Q_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^2-\sum_{j=1}^q x_{p+j}^2$, write $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0$ for the even part of the canonical $\mathbb Z/2$ grading. If $p>0$, then

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. For the standard complex form $Q_n(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$ with $n>0$, the even subalgebra is isomorphic over $\mathbb C$ to $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n-1}(\mathbb C)$, the complex Clifford algebra on $n-1$ generators each having square $-1$, and hence to the standard complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.

Let $n=p+q$, let $r$ be the residue of $p-q$ modulo $8$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and use $v^2=Q(v)1$ with signature ordered $(+^p,-^q)$. For every nondegenerate real form of signature $(p,q)$, the real Clifford algebra is

| $r$ | parity of $n$ | $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}$ |
|---:|:---:|---|
| $0$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $1$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, compactness makes the discrete manifold $M$ finite. The $H^1$ and $L^2$ spaces are the same finite direct sums of fibers, and $D_V^+=0:\bigoplus_xV_x^+\to\bigoplus_xV_x^-$ because $T^*M=0$. Its kernel and cokernel are those two finite direct sums, so its index is $\sum_x(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-)$. The reference grading in the Statement gives $\operatorname{str}_{W_x}I=\varepsilon_x(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-)$, while $\widehat A_0=1$ and $F^{V/S}=0$. The signed integration rule [F6] therefore gives $\int_M[\widehat A\operatorname{ch}(V/S)]_0=\sum_x\varepsilon_x^2(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-)=\operatorname{ind}(D_V^+)$. This includes negative points, mixtures of signs, arbitrary fiber gradings, rank-zero fibers and the empty manifold.

Suppose $m\ge1$. By [F1], $D_V^+$ is a Fredholm operator on the stated exact domain. For each $t>0$, [F2] makes $e^{-tD_V^2}$ trace class and gives $\operatorname{ind}(D_V^+)=\operatorname{Tr}(\Gamma_Ve^{-tD_V^2})=\int_M\operatorname{str}K_t(x,x)\,d\operatorname{vol}_g(x)$, where $\Gamma_V$ is $+1$ on $V^+$ and $-1$ on $V^-$.

In each normal-coordinate neighborhood, [F3] replaces $K_t$ by its finite heat parametrix with a remainder $O(t^N)$ in the diagonal $C^0$ norm for any prescribed $N$, after increasing the truncation order. Since $M$ is compact, the volume is finite, so the integral of that remainder tends to zero. By [F4], $\operatorname{str}u_j(x,x)=0$ for $j<m$. In $(4\pi t)^{-m}\sum_jt^ju_j(x,x)$ each smooth coefficient with $j>m$ is multiplied by $t^{j-m}$ and tends uniformly to zero. Within $u_m$, only Clifford degree $2m$ contributes to supertrace. Thus the limit of the diagonal supertrace integral as $t\downarrow0$ is the integral of its single degree-$2m$ oscillator coefficient.

By [F5], that coefficient is the form $[\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})\operatorname{ch}(V/S)]_{2m}$. Taking the limit in the $t$-independent identity of step 1.2 proves the displayed index formula. The result is computed over the complex Hilbert spaces $L^2(V^\pm)$, so no conclusion about real KO-index groups follows. The empty manifold has zero domain and codomain and both sides are zero; the zero-dimensional case is computed in step 1.1, and no boundary condition is needed because $M$ has no boundary.

| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold of dimension $2m$ and let $\Omega^{LC}$ be the skew-symmetric matrix of curvature two-forms of the Levi–Civita connection, with curvature convention
$R(X,Y)=[\nabla_X,\nabla_Y]-\nabla_{[X,Y]}$.
Define
$$\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})=\det{}^{1/2}\!\left(\frac{i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi}{\sinh(i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi)}\right).$$
The determinant and square root are formal power series in commuting even-degree differential forms; the square-root branch has constant term $1$, and terms above degree $2m$ are discarded. This is the normalization of the A-hat characteristic form in [[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]].

For $m\ge1$ and a graded Hermitian Clifford module $V$ with compatible connection, use the local multiplicity space and relative curvature from [[lem-spinor-and-clifford-associated-bundles-are-well-defined]]. Define the **relative Chern character form** by
$$
\operatorname{ch}(V/S)=\operatorname{str}_{W}\exp\!\left(-\frac{F^{V/S}}{2\pi i}\right).
$$
Here $\operatorname{str}$ is the ordinary trace if $W$ is ungraded and the even trace minus odd trace if it is graded. The cited well-definedness lemma proves this local expression patches to a global even form. For $V=S\widehat\otimes E$ with the product connection, it is $\operatorname{tr}\exp(-F^E/(2\pi i))$. The Chern–Weil supplier [[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]] identifies the resulting cohomology classes after passage to real coefficients; this definition asserts no integral torsion identity.

For $m=0$, let $\varepsilon_x\in\{1,-1\}$ be the supplied orientation sign at $x$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). The reference zero-dimensional Clifford module $S_{0,x}$ is the complex line with grading operator $\Gamma_{S_{0,x}}=\varepsilon_x I$: it is even at a positive point and odd at a negative point. The zero-dimensional Clifford algebra is $\mathbb C$, acting by scalars. Set $W_x=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S_{0,x},V_x)$ with the grading for which evaluation $S_{0,x}\widehat\otimes W_x\to V_x$ is even. Identifying a map with its value at $1$ gives $\Gamma_{W_x}=\varepsilon_x\Gamma_{V_x}$. All curvature two-forms vanish, so $\widehat A_0=1$, $F^{V/S}=0$, and
$$\operatorname{ch}(V/S)_0(x)=\operatorname{str}_{W_x}I=\varepsilon_x\bigl(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-\bigr).$$
This formula is independent of any basis of $V_x$ and leaves its arbitrary given grading unrestricted. For $V=S_0\widehat\otimes E$ with $E$ in even degree, evaluation identifies $W=E$ in even degree, so the relative character is the ordinary rank, consistently with the product formula above. This reference-line convention makes no assertion about a Spin$(0)$ lift or its isomorphism classes.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, compactness makes $M$ a finite discrete set. By [F4], the chiral operator is the zero map $\bigoplus_{\varepsilon_x=1}E_x\to\bigoplus_{\varepsilon_x=-1}E_x$, so it is Fredholm with index $\sum_x\varepsilon_x\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}E_x$. All curvature two-forms vanish; $\widehat A_0=1$ and the ordinary Chern character is the rank. The signed integral in [F4] is therefore this same sum, and [F3] agrees because the multiplicity bundle is $E$ in even degree. No Spin$(0)$ lift or torsor classification is asserted. The argument includes both point signs, disconnected mixtures, rank-zero twists and the empty manifold.

Suppose $m\ge1$. The tensor-product connection is unitary and Clifford-compatible, and the product grading is the spinor chirality grading tensored with the even grading on $E$. Hence [F3] applies to $V$ and gives a Fredholm chiral operator with index equal to the integral of $\widehat A$ times its relative Chern character.

By [F2], the relative curvature for this product is exactly $F^E$, and the relative supertrace is the ordinary trace because $E$ is ungraded. Substituting this equality in [F3] gives the displayed formula. If $E$ has rank zero, the module, both $L^2$ spaces, and the trace form are zero. The result uses the exact suppliers in [A1]; it remains a complex index.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold of even dimension $2m$, and let $V=V^+\oplus V^-$ be a finite-rank smooth complex vector bundle with a Hermitian metric linear in its first variable. Write $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathbb C}(T^*M,-g)$ for the complex Clifford bundle generated by cotangent vectors with relation $\xi\eta+\eta\xi=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)$. A **graded Hermitian Clifford action** is a smooth real-linear map $c:T^*M\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ such that $c(\xi)^*=-c(\xi)$, $c(\xi)V^\pm\subseteq V^\mp$, and $c(\xi)c(\eta)+c(\eta)c(\xi)=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)I$. It extends complex-linearly to the complex Clifford bundle.

A **graded Hermitian Clifford connection** is a unitary connection $\nabla^V$ preserving $V^\pm$ and satisfying
$$\nabla^V_X(c(\xi)v)=c(\nabla^{LC}_X\xi)v+c(\xi)\nabla^V_Xv$$
for smooth $X,\xi,v$, where $\nabla^{LC}$ is the Levi–Civita connection. In a local orthonormal coframe $(e^i)$ define
$$D_Vv=\sum_i c(e^i)\nabla^V_{e_i}v.$$
The operator is odd, so its chiral part is $D_V^+:C^\infty(V^+)\to C^\infty(V^-)$. The formula's frame independence, formal symmetry on closed $M$, and global bundle well-definedness are proved in [[lem-geometric-dirac-operator-is-well-defined]]. A domain and index are assigned only under the compact hypotheses of later items.

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under the unitary Fourier transform [F2], $D$ is multiplication by the matrix $2\pi i c(\xi)$. Its maximal multiplier domain is $\{u:|\xi|\widehat u\in L^2\}=H^1$, because [F1] gives $|c(\xi)v|=|\xi||v|$; a multiplication operator by a measurable finite matrix is closed, since convergence of $u_k$ and $c(\xi)u_k$ in $L^2$ has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence and the pointwise multiplication identity passes to the limit. Schwartz sections are dense in $L^2$, so $D$ is densely defined and closed.

If $h$ is orthogonal to the range, then distributionally $D^*h=0$. Fourier transformation and [F2] give $c(\xi)\widehat h(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. By [F1], $c(\xi)$ is invertible for every $\xi\ne0$, and the singleton $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero; hence $\widehat h=0$ almost everywhere and $h=0$. Thus the range is dense.

Fix a unit vector $v\in S_0$ and define $\widehat g(\xi)=\mathbf 1_{\{0<|\xi|<1\}}|\xi|^{-(n/2-1)}v$. Polar coordinates give $\|\widehat g\|_2^2=C_n\int_0^1 r^{n-1-2(n/2-1)}\,dr=C_n\int_0^1r\,dr<\infty$, so [F2] gives $g\in L^2$. If $g=Du$ for some $u\in H^1$, then for almost every $\xi\ne0$, [F1] forces $|\widehat u(\xi)|=(2\pi)^{-1}|\xi|^{-1}|\widehat g(\xi)|$. Consequently its squared norm near zero is a positive constant times $\int_0^1r^{n-1-2(n/2)}\,dr=\int_0^1r^{-1}\,dr=\infty$, contradicting $u\in L^2$. Thus $g$ is not in the range, so the dense range is proper and not closed. A Fredholm operator must have closed range, hence $D$ is not Fredholm.

The construction works also for $n=1$, where the exponent in $\widehat g$ is $1/2$ and the displayed $L^2$ integral is still finite; the logarithmic divergence after division by $|\xi|$ is unchanged. The zero-frequency set has measure zero, but arbitrarily small nonzero frequencies cause the obstruction. Countable choice is used only through [A1] and [F2].

Assume AC, inherited from the characteristic-class and bundle-splitting
suppliers. Let $n\ge0$, let $\gamma\to\mathbb{CP}^n$ be the tautological complex
line, and let $x=c_1(\gamma^*)$. With the complex orientation of
$\mathbb{CP}^n$, $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{n+1})$ and
$\langle x^n,[\mathbb{CP}^n]\rangle=1$. There is a canonical Euler short exact
sequence of complex vector bundles
$$0\longrightarrow\underline{\mathbb C}\xrightarrow{\iota}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\gamma,\underline{\mathbb C}^{n+1})\xrightarrow{q}T\mathbb{CP}^n\longrightarrow0,$$
whose middle term is canonically $(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$. The first map
sends a scalar to that scalar times the inclusion of the represented line; the
second is induced by the quotient $\mathbb C^{n+1}\to\mathbb C^{n+1}/\gamma$. A
bundle metric supplies a splitting, giving a complex bundle isomorphism
$\underline{\mathbb C}\oplus T\mathbb{CP}^n\cong(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$
without asserting a canonical direct-sum splitting. Consequently
$$c(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x)^{n+1},\qquad p(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x^2)^{n+1}$$
in the truncated integral cohomology ring, and
$p_k(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=\binom{n+1}{k}x^{2k}$, with all terms above the manifold
dimension zero. In particular
$$p_k[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}]=\binom{2k+1}{k},$$
including $p_1[\mathbb{CP}^2]=3$, $p_2[\mathbb{CP}^4]=10$, and the rank-zero
convention $p_0[\mathbb{CP}^0]=1$.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle over a
path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex and let $\rho_2$ denote reduction
of coefficients modulo two. Then
$$w_{2i+1}(E_{\mathbb R})=0,\qquad w_{2i}(E_{\mathbb R})=\rho_2c_i(E) \qquad(i\geq0),$$
where $w$ denotes the total Stiefel-Whitney class of the underlying real
bundle.

Fix the coordinate flag
$0\subset\mathbb F^1\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb F^N$. A **Schubert symbol**
for $\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$ is a strictly increasing sequence
$a=(a_1<\cdots<a_n)$ with $1\leq a_i\leq N$. Its **Schubert cell** is

$$e(a)=\{W:\dim(W\cap\mathbb F^{a_i})=i,\ \dim(W\cap\mathbb F^{a_i-1})=i-1\text{ for every }i\}.$$

Every $W\in e(a)$ has a unique pivot-normalized basis

$$v_i=e_{a_i}+\sum_{\substack{j<a_i\\j\notin\{a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1}\}}}x_{ij}e_j,$$

after using earlier pivot rows to clear their columns. The free coordinates
number

$$d(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-i),$$

so $e(a)\cong\mathbb F^{d(a)}$. Its real dimension is $d(a)$ for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and $2d(a)$ for $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$.
Equivalently, the integers $a_i-i$, read in reverse order, form a partition
fitting the $n$ by $(N-n)$ rectangle. These spaces use the Grassmannian
topology fixed in
[[def-stiefel-space-grassmannian-and-tautological-bundle]].
For $n=0$, the unique symbol is the empty sequence, the displayed sum is the
empty sum $0$, and its Schubert cell is the one-point Grassmannian.

The Schubert strata are open cells whose closures are unions of cells with
componentwise smaller pivot symbols. They form a finite CW structure on
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)$, and the standard inclusions
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^N)\to
\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^{N+1})$ are cellular subcomplex inclusions.
Their union is the stated CW structure on
$\operatorname{Gr}_n(\mathbb F^\infty)$, and each finite-dimensional
subcomplex is contained in a finite stage.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

For a space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, a degree-$n$ **singular cocycle** is a cochain in $Z^n(X;G)=\ker\delta^n$ and a degree-$n$ **singular coboundary** belongs to $B^n(X;G)=\operatorname{im}\delta^{n-1}$, for the positive coboundary convention of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. The square-zero lemma [[lem-the-singular-coboundary-squares-to-zero]] implies $B^n\subseteq Z^n$: if $\varphi=\delta^{n-1}\psi$, then $\delta^n\varphi=0$.

The **singular cohomology group with coefficients in $G$** is
$$H^n(X;G)=Z^n(X;G)/B^n(X;G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad H^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0).$$
This is the abelian quotient with addition $[\varphi]+[\psi]=[\varphi+\psi]$: changing either representative by a coboundary changes the sum by a coboundary. Thus two cocycles represent the same class exactly when their difference is $\delta^{n-1}\eta$ for some degree-$(n-1)$ cochain $\eta$. In degree zero, $B^0=0$ because $C^{-1}=0$; hence $H^0=\ker\delta^0$. The zero convention in negative degrees agrees with the same kernel/image construction on the zero cochain groups.

If coefficients are a module over a commutative ring, the same groups and maps are modules and linear maps, and this is their module quotient. Empty $X$ or zero coefficients give zero cohomology in every degree. The notation does not define cohomology as the dual of homology; such identifications require their own theorems. No choice of cocycle representatives and no AC is part of this definition.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $E\to M$ be an oriented Euclidean smooth real vector bundle of rank $n\ge1$ over a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold. Then $E$ admits a Spin lift of [[def-spin-lift-of-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]] if and only if $w_2(E)=0\in H^2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. When nonempty, isomorphism classes of lifts form a torsor under $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$: twisting a lift by a principal $\{\pm1\}$-bundle gives a free and transitive action. No distinguished lift is asserted. Rank zero is excluded.

derivations.claim: By [F1] with $n=2$, $c_1(T\mathbb{CP}^2)=3x$. The coefficient reduction $\rho_2$ is a ring homomorphism, so $\rho_2(3x)=\rho_2(x)$ because $3\equiv1\pmod2$.

The CW structure in [F4] has cellular chains $C_4\cong\mathbb Z$, $C_2\cong\mathbb Z$, and $C_0\cong\mathbb Z$, with all other groups zero. Every cellular boundary is zero because its target is zero, so cellular and singular homology give $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ and $H_1=0$. By UCT with integral coefficients, evaluation identifies $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)$; since $x$ is an integral cohomology generator by [F2], it evaluates as $+1$ or $-1$ on a homology generator. UCT with $\mathbb F_2$ coefficients identifies $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb F_2)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)$, and naturality of coefficient reduction makes $\rho_2(x)$ evaluate as $1$. Hence $\rho_2(x)\ne0$.

Applying [F3] to the complex tangent bundle and using steps 1.1–1.2 gives $w_2(T\mathbb{CP}^2)=\rho_2(x)\ne0$. The manifold is complex-oriented, hence its tangent bundle is oriented; [F5] therefore implies that it admits no Spin lift. The coefficient group has characteristic two and no sign convention changes the nonzero class.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold of even dimension $n=2m\ge2$ with a specified Spin lift $P\to P_{SO}(TM)$. Let $S_0$ be the complex irreducible Clifford module of dimension $2^m$ supplied by [[thm-complex-spin-modules-and-compact-reducibility]], with positive-square complex Clifford action $c_+$ and full-even Spin representation $\sigma$. Put $c_0(v)=i\,c_+(v)$ for the negative-square cotangent action. This changes the Clifford square sign and preserves equivariance under $\sigma$, since the scalar $i$ commutes with that action. Define the complex spinor bundle by the associated real bundle $P\times_{\operatorname{Spin}(n)}(S_0)_{\mathbb R}$ using the realification of $\sigma$, and descend multiplication by $i$ and the Clifford action through their commuting transition maps.

For an oriented orthonormal basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_{2m})$, define the chirality operator on $S_0$ by $\Gamma_{S_0}=i^m c_0(e^1)\cdots c_0(e^{2m})$. The calculation below proves that this is basis-independent, squares to $1$, and anticommutes with each $c_0(\xi)$. Its $\pm1$ eigenspaces are $S_0^\pm$ and their associated bundles are $S^\pm$. The Levi–Civita connection on $P_{SO}(TM)$ lifts through the differential of $\operatorname{Spin}(n)\to SO(n)$ to the **spin connection** $\widetilde\nabla^S$ on $S$. This item defines these objects; [[lem-spinor-and-clifford-associated-bundles-are-well-defined]] supplies the global bundle, metric, connection, and transition verification.

Assume full AC. On an even-dimensional oriented Riemannian manifold with a supplied Spin lift, the realified associated construction in [[def-even-dimensional-spinor-bundle-chirality-and-spin-connection]] is a smooth Hermitian graded Clifford bundle with a global compatible spin connection. For any graded Hermitian Clifford module there is locally a graded factorization $V\cong S_0\widehat\otimes W$. Its local multiplicity spaces $W=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cl}}(S_0,V)$ and the relative curvature $F^{V/S}:=F^V-c(R^{LC})$ have transition laws for which $\operatorname{str}_W\exp(-F^{V/S}/(2\pi i))$ is a global even form. In the spin-twisted case $V=S\widehat\otimes E$, this relative curvature is the curvature $F^E$ of the supplied unitary connection. For the zero-dimensional relative statement, use the orientation-graded reference line of [[def-ahat-and-relative-chern-character-forms]]; this does not construct a Spin$(0)$ lift.

Use the complex PA-04 Clifford classification in [A1] and [A2]. For the complexification of a positive-definite real $n$-space, the irreducible Clifford spinor modules and their restrictions to full-even Spin are as follows:

- If $n=2m$ with $m\ge1$, the unique irreducible complex Clifford module has dimension $2^m$; its restriction to Spin is $S^+\oplus S^-$, with two inequivalent irreducible half-spin modules of dimension $2^{m-1}$ each.
- If $n=2m+1$, there are two inequivalent irreducible complex Clifford modules, each of dimension $2^m$; their restrictions to Spin are isomorphic to the same irreducible complex Spin module of dimension $2^m$.
- For $n=0$, there is one one-dimensional complex Clifford spinor; for $n=1$, there are two one-dimensional Clifford spinors and their restrictions to $\operatorname{Spin}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ agree.

Separately, assuming AC, every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of the compact Hausdorff group $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is completely reducible. This applies to all finite-dimensional continuous representations, not only the spinor modules above.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $G$ be a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group.

(1) If $G$ is compact with $m_G(G)=1$, its dual $\widehat G$ is discrete and the compatible dual Haar measure gives each point mass $1$; the Plancherel theorem then reads as the Fourier-series identity $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\gamma)|^2,\qquad f\in L^2(G).$$

(2) If $G$ is discrete with $m_G$ the counting measure (each point of mass $1$), then $\widehat G$ is compact and the compatible dual Haar measure is the normalised Haar measure of $\widehat G$, and Plancherel reads $$\sum_{x\in G}|f(x)|^2=\|\widehat f\|_2^2,\qquad f\in\ell^2(G).$$

Without the stated normalisation of $m_G$ the identification of the dual measure in (2) is false; the compatible scale is reciprocal in $m_G$, as [[thm-compatible-dual-haar-normalisation]] records. For a general $L^2$ function, $\widehat f$ denotes the Plancherel transform $\mathcal Ff$; its pointwise integral formula is asserted only when $f\in L^1$.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

(1) For locally compact Hausdorff abelian groups $G_{1},\dots,G_{n}$ the map
$$\Phi:\widehat{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_{n}}\to\widehat{G_{1}\times\cdots\times G_{n}},\qquad \Phi(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n})\big((x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big):=\prod_{j}\gamma_{j}(x_{j}),$$
is an isomorphism of topological groups for the product topologies (choice-free,
finite $n$). (2) If $(G_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of discrete abelian groups and
$G=\bigoplus_{i}G_{i}$ is their algebraic direct sum equipped with the discrete
topology ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]), then, assuming the Axiom
of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), $\widehat G$ is topologically isomorphic to
the product $\prod_{i}\widehat{G_{i}}$ with the product topology. No claim is
made here about a direct sum carrying the subspace topology of the product of
non-discrete factors.

Assume full AC and the closed hypotheses of [[lem-dirac-maximal-domain-is-h1]]. The chiral operator
$$D_V^+:H^1(V^+)\longrightarrow L^2(V^-)$$
is Fredholm. Its kernel is $\ker D_V\cap L^2(V^+)$, its cokernel is canonically $\ker D_V\cap L^2(V^-)$, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_V^+=\dim\ker D_V^+-\dim\ker D_V^-.$$
Both kernels are finite-dimensional and consist of smooth sections.

Use the plus-square convention $v^2=Q(v)1$. For the real standard form $Q_{p,q}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p x_i^2-\sum_{j=1}^q x_{p+j}^2$, write $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0$ for the even part of the canonical $\mathbb Z/2$ grading. If $p>0$, then

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. For the standard complex form $Q_n(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$ with $n>0$, the even subalgebra is isomorphic over $\mathbb C$ to $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n-1}(\mathbb C)$, the complex Clifford algebra on $n-1$ generators each having square $-1$, and hence to the standard complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}_{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.

Let $n=p+q$, let $r$ be the residue of $p-q$ modulo $8$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$, and use $v^2=Q(v)1$ with signature ordered $(+^p,-^q)$. For every nondegenerate real form of signature $(p,q)$, the real Clifford algebra is

| $r$ | parity of $n$ | $\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}$ |
|---:|:---:|---|
| $0$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $1$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $2$ | even | $M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb R)$ |
| $3$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |
| $4$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $5$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)\oplus M_{2^{(n-3)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $6$ | even | $M_{2^{(n-2)/2}}(\mathbb H)$ |
| $7$ | odd | $M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)$ |

Only signatures with $p,q\ge0$ are considered; in the feasible rows the displayed exponents are nonnegative. For a nondegenerate complex quadratic form on dimension $n$, its Clifford algebra is

$$\mathrm{Cl}_n(\mathbb C)\cong\begin{cases}M_{2^{n/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ even},\\M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C)\oplus M_{2^{(n-1)/2}}(\mathbb C),&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}$$

These matrix-algebra classifications require nondegeneracy; no such classification is asserted for degenerate forms.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: First classify the characters of $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. If $\chi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ is a continuous character, let $f(t)=\chi([t])$. By continuity at $0$, choose $\delta>0$ so that on $|t|<2\delta$ the values of $f$ lie in the arc with a continuous argument $\theta(t)\in(-1/8,1/8)$, normalized by $f(t)=e^{2\pi i\theta(t)}$. Whenever $|s|,|t|,|s+t|<\delta$, the character identity gives $\theta(s+t)-\theta(s)-\theta(t)\in\mathbb Z$; this difference has absolute value less than $3/8$, so it is zero. Define $\Theta(u)=N\theta(u/N)$ for any positive integer $N$ with $|u/N|<\delta$. If $N,N'$ both work, repeated local additivity gives $N\theta(u/N)=NN'\theta(u/(NN'))=N'\theta(u/N')$, so $\Theta$ is well-defined. Choosing $N$ large enough for $s,t,s+t$ shows $\Theta(s+t)=\Theta(s)+\Theta(t)$. Near zero $\Theta=\theta$, so $\Theta$ is continuous, and the continuous additive equation gives $\Theta(t)=\alpha t$ for some $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. For arbitrary $t$, choose $N$ with $|t/N|<\delta$; then $f(t)=f(t/N)^N=e^{2\pi i\alpha t}$. Since $f(1)=1$, $\alpha\in\mathbb Z$. Conversely each $k\in\mathbb Z$ defines $\chi_k([t])=e^{2\pi i kt}$, so $\widehat{\mathbb T}=\mathbb Z$. Finite-product duality now identifies the frequencies of $\mathbb T^{2m}$ with $\mathbb Z^{2m}$, and compact-group Plancherel makes these characters a complete orthonormal basis.

The quotient $\mathbb R^{2m}/\mathbb Z^{2m}$ has a global parallel coframe, so the Levi–Civita connection and the periodic spin connection have zero local connection matrix. For each $k\in\mathbb Z^{2m}$, the Fourier character $e_k(x)=e^{2\pi i k\cdot x}$ satisfies $D(e_k\otimes s)=2\pi i\,e_k\otimes c(k)s$. For $k\ne0$, $c(k)^2=-|k|^2I$, so $c(k)$ is invertible.

By the completeness in [F3], every $L^2$ spinor is determined by its Fourier coefficients. The equation $D\psi=0$ forces every nonzero-frequency coefficient to vanish by step 1.2; the zero-frequency coefficient is arbitrary. Thus $\ker D^+$ consists exactly of constant elements of $S^+$, and $\ker(D^+)^*=\ker D^-$ consists exactly of constants in $S^-$.

By [F2], $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^+=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^-=2^{m-1}$. Hence the Fredholm index supplied by [F4] is $\dim\ker D^+-\dim\ker(D^+)^*=2^{m-1}-2^{m-1}=0$. For $m=1$ both dimensions are one; the zero-dimensional torus is outside the stated range $m\ge1$. The half-spin dimensions use the exact algebra suppliers in [A1].

Assume AC, inherited from the characteristic-class and bundle-splitting
suppliers. Let $n\ge0$, let $\gamma\to\mathbb{CP}^n$ be the tautological complex
line, and let $x=c_1(\gamma^*)$. With the complex orientation of
$\mathbb{CP}^n$, $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{n+1})$ and
$\langle x^n,[\mathbb{CP}^n]\rangle=1$. There is a canonical Euler short exact
sequence of complex vector bundles
$$0\longrightarrow\underline{\mathbb C}\xrightarrow{\iota}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\gamma,\underline{\mathbb C}^{n+1})\xrightarrow{q}T\mathbb{CP}^n\longrightarrow0,$$
whose middle term is canonically $(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$. The first map
sends a scalar to that scalar times the inclusion of the represented line; the
second is induced by the quotient $\mathbb C^{n+1}\to\mathbb C^{n+1}/\gamma$. A
bundle metric supplies a splitting, giving a complex bundle isomorphism
$\underline{\mathbb C}\oplus T\mathbb{CP}^n\cong(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$
without asserting a canonical direct-sum splitting. Consequently
$$c(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x)^{n+1},\qquad p(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x^2)^{n+1}$$
in the truncated integral cohomology ring, and
$p_k(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=\binom{n+1}{k}x^{2k}$, with all terms above the manifold
dimension zero. In particular
$$p_k[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}]=\binom{2k+1}{k},$$
including $p_1[\mathbb{CP}^2]=3$, $p_2[\mathbb{CP}^4]=10$, and the rank-zero
convention $p_0[\mathbb{CP}^0]=1$.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle over a
path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex and let $\rho_2$ denote reduction
of coefficients modulo two. Then
$$w_{2i+1}(E_{\mathbb R})=0,\qquad w_{2i}(E_{\mathbb R})=\rho_2c_i(E) \qquad(i\geq0),$$
where $w$ denotes the total Stiefel-Whitney class of the underlying real
bundle.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $E\to M$ be an oriented Euclidean smooth real vector bundle of rank $n\ge1$ over a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold. Then $E$ admits a Spin lift of [[def-spin-lift-of-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]] if and only if $w_2(E)=0\in H^2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. When nonempty, isomorphism classes of lifts form a torsor under $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$: twisting a lift by a principal $\{\pm1\}$-bundle gives a free and transitive action. No distinguished lift is asserted. Rank zero is excluded.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-sectional-curvature]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $r>0$. For $n\ge2$, the round sphere

$$S^n_r=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:|x|=r\}$$

with its metric induced from Euclidean space has constant sectional curvature
$1/r^2$. For $n=0$ or $n=1$, its sectional-curvature domain is empty.

The choice assumption is inherited through both the smooth orthogonal
projection constructions used by the Gauss–Weingarten suppliers and the
sectional-curvature interface.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold
it gives the unique zero four-tensor; in dimension one the same formula applies
and later symmetries force it to vanish. It is valid up to the boundary when a
Riemannian manifold with boundary is supplied.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless even-dimensional Spin Riemannian manifold, and suppose its scalar curvature satisfies $\operatorname{scal}_g(x)>0$ for every $x\in M$. Then every smooth untwisted spinor $\psi$ satisfying $D_S\psi=0$ is zero.

The sectional curvature is $1$ by [F3]. In an orthonormal frame on a surface, scalar curvature is $R_{1221}+R_{2112}=2$, with the sign convention of [F3]. It is strictly positive everywhere.

Apply [F4] to the Spin structure from step 1.1 and the positive scalar curvature from step 1.2. Every smooth untwisted harmonic spinor is zero. The assertion is for the untwisted operator; a line twist has its own curvature term and is treated separately.

Assume AC, inherited from the characteristic-class and bundle-splitting
suppliers. Let $n\ge0$, let $\gamma\to\mathbb{CP}^n$ be the tautological complex
line, and let $x=c_1(\gamma^*)$. With the complex orientation of
$\mathbb{CP}^n$, $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{n+1})$ and
$\langle x^n,[\mathbb{CP}^n]\rangle=1$. There is a canonical Euler short exact
sequence of complex vector bundles
$$0\longrightarrow\underline{\mathbb C}\xrightarrow{\iota}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\gamma,\underline{\mathbb C}^{n+1})\xrightarrow{q}T\mathbb{CP}^n\longrightarrow0,$$
whose middle term is canonically $(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$. The first map
sends a scalar to that scalar times the inclusion of the represented line; the
second is induced by the quotient $\mathbb C^{n+1}\to\mathbb C^{n+1}/\gamma$. A
bundle metric supplies a splitting, giving a complex bundle isomorphism
$\underline{\mathbb C}\oplus T\mathbb{CP}^n\cong(\gamma^*)^{\oplus(n+1)}$
without asserting a canonical direct-sum splitting. Consequently
$$c(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x)^{n+1},\qquad p(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=(1+x^2)^{n+1}$$
in the truncated integral cohomology ring, and
$p_k(T\mathbb{CP}^n)=\binom{n+1}{k}x^{2k}$, with all terms above the manifold
dimension zero. In particular
$$p_k[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}]=\binom{2k+1}{k},$$
including $p_1[\mathbb{CP}^2]=3$, $p_2[\mathbb{CP}^4]=10$, and the rank-zero
convention $p_0[\mathbb{CP}^0]=1$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle over a
path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex and let $\rho_2$ denote reduction
of coefficients modulo two. Then
$$w_{2i+1}(E_{\mathbb R})=0,\qquad w_{2i}(E_{\mathbb R})=\rho_2c_i(E) \qquad(i\geq0),$$
where $w$ denotes the total Stiefel-Whitney class of the underlying real
bundle.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $E\to M$ be an oriented Euclidean smooth real vector bundle of rank $n\ge1$ over a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold. Then $E$ admits a Spin lift of [[def-spin-lift-of-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]] if and only if $w_2(E)=0\in H^2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. When nonempty, isomorphism classes of lifts form a torsor under $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$: twisting a lift by a principal $\{\pm1\}$-bundle gives a free and transitive action. No distinguished lift is asserted. Rank zero is excluded.

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold of dimension $2m$ and let $\Omega^{LC}$ be the skew-symmetric matrix of curvature two-forms of the Levi–Civita connection, with curvature convention
$R(X,Y)=[\nabla_X,\nabla_Y]-\nabla_{[X,Y]}$.
Define
$$\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})=\det{}^{1/2}\!\left(\frac{i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi}{\sinh(i\Omega^{LC}/4\pi)}\right).$$
The determinant and square root are formal power series in commuting even-degree differential forms; the square-root branch has constant term $1$, and terms above degree $2m$ are discarded. This is the normalization of the A-hat characteristic form in [[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]].

For $m\ge1$ and a graded Hermitian Clifford module $V$ with compatible connection, use the local multiplicity space and relative curvature from [[lem-spinor-and-clifford-associated-bundles-are-well-defined]]. Define the **relative Chern character form** by
$$
\operatorname{ch}(V/S)=\operatorname{str}_{W}\exp\!\left(-\frac{F^{V/S}}{2\pi i}\right).
$$
Here $\operatorname{str}$ is the ordinary trace if $W$ is ungraded and the even trace minus odd trace if it is graded. The cited well-definedness lemma proves this local expression patches to a global even form. For $V=S\widehat\otimes E$ with the product connection, it is $\operatorname{tr}\exp(-F^E/(2\pi i))$. The Chern–Weil supplier [[thm-chern-weil-forms-represent-the-at-characteristic-classes-over-the-reals]] identifies the resulting cohomology classes after passage to real coefficients; this definition asserts no integral torsion identity.

For $m=0$, let $\varepsilon_x\in\{1,-1\}$ be the supplied orientation sign at $x$ ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]). The reference zero-dimensional Clifford module $S_{0,x}$ is the complex line with grading operator $\Gamma_{S_{0,x}}=\varepsilon_x I$: it is even at a positive point and odd at a negative point. The zero-dimensional Clifford algebra is $\mathbb C$, acting by scalars. Set $W_x=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(S_{0,x},V_x)$ with the grading for which evaluation $S_{0,x}\widehat\otimes W_x\to V_x$ is even. Identifying a map with its value at $1$ gives $\Gamma_{W_x}=\varepsilon_x\Gamma_{V_x}$. All curvature two-forms vanish, so $\widehat A_0=1$, $F^{V/S}=0$, and
$$\operatorname{ch}(V/S)_0(x)=\operatorname{str}_{W_x}I=\varepsilon_x\bigl(\dim V_x^+-\dim V_x^-\bigr).$$
This formula is independent of any basis of $V_x$ and leaves its arbitrary given grading unrestricted. For $V=S_0\widehat\otimes E$ with $E$ in even degree, evaluation identifies $W=E$ in even degree, so the relative character is the ordinary rank, consistently with the product formula above. This reference-line convention makes no assertion about a Spin$(0)$ lift or its isomorphism classes.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold,
possibly with boundary. If $E\to M$ is a rank-$r$ complex vector bundle with
complex connection $\nabla$ and curvature $\Omega$, define the total Chern form
$$c(\nabla)=\det\!\left(I-\frac{\Omega}{2\pi i}\right)=\sum_{j=0}^r c_j(\nabla),$$
where $c_j(\nabla)$ has degree $2j$. For a Hermitian connection these forms
are real-valued; a general complex connection need not give real-valued forms.

For a rank-$r$ real vector bundle with real connection $\nabla$, let
$E_{\mathbb C}=E\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ carry the complexified
connection $\nabla_{\mathbb C}$ and set
$$p_j(\nabla)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})\quad\text{in degree }4j,\qquad p(\nabla)=\sum_{j\geq0}p_j(\nabla).$$
Then $p_0=1$, $p_j=0$ when $2j>r$, and every $p_j(\nabla)$ is real-valued,
even if $\nabla$ is not metric-compatible. If $\nabla$ is compatible with a
Euclidean metric, each odd Chern form $c_{2j+1}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})$ vanishes
pointwise. Assume full Axiom of Choice (AC); for every real connection each
$c_{2j+1}(\nabla_{\mathbb C})$ is then exact, with AC used through existence
of a metric-compatible connection and the transgression lemma.

If $E$ is an oriented Euclidean bundle of even rank $2m$ and $\nabla$ is
metric-compatible, define
$$e(\nabla)=\operatorname{Pf}\!\left(\frac{\Omega}{2\pi}\right),$$
where the Pfaffian uses the ordered oriented orthonormal frame and
$\operatorname{Pf}\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)=a$.
These curvature evaluations are closed forms. In rank zero,
$c(\nabla)=p(\nabla)=e(\nabla)=1$. The Euler form is defined here only for
oriented even-rank Euclidean bundles with a metric-compatible connection.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$\rho_M:H^*(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^*(M;\mathbb R)$ be induced by
$\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Write $J_M$ for the natural de Rham
isomorphism from real de Rham cohomology to singular cohomology with real
coefficients.

For every finite-rank smooth complex bundle $E\to M$ with a Hermitian metric
and Hermitian connection $\nabla$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([c_j(\nabla)])=\rho_M(c_j(E)).$$
For every finite-rank smooth real bundle $V\to M$ with any real connection
$D$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([p_j(D)])=\rho_M(p_j(V)).$$
For every oriented Euclidean bundle $W\to M$ of even rank with a
metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, and its Thom-normalized Euler class,
$$J_M([e(\nabla)])=\rho_M(e(W)).$$
Here $c_j(\nabla)$, $p_j(D)$, and $e(\nabla)$ use the normalizations in
[[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]], while $c_j(E)$,
$p_j(V)$, and $e(W)$ are the published topological classes. In particular
$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for a complex line and
$p_j(V)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(V_{\mathbb C})$. These are equalities after passage to
real coefficients; no equality with integral torsion is asserted.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact, boundaryless, oriented, Riemannian manifold of even dimension $2m$ with $m\ge0$, and let $E\to M$ be any finite-rank complex Hermitian vector bundle with a unitary connection. For $m\ge1$, assume a specified Spin lift and use the ordinary chiral Spinor bundle. For $m=0$, no Spin lift is input: at a point with orientation sign $\varepsilon_x$, use the reference line from [[def-ahat-and-relative-chern-character-forms]], in even degree for $\varepsilon_x=1$ and odd degree for $\varepsilon_x=-1$. Thus $D^+_{S\otimes E}=0:\bigoplus_{\varepsilon_x=1}E_x\to\bigoplus_{\varepsilon_x=-1}E_x$. Then the chiral operator is Fredholm and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}(D^+_{S\otimes E})=\int_M\left[\widehat A(TM,\nabla^{LC})\operatorname{tr}\exp\!\left(-\frac{F^E}{2\pi i}\right)\right]_{2m}.$$
The rank-zero twist gives index and integral both equal to zero. The zero-dimensional convention does not assert an unstabilized Spin$(0)$ lift or assign it an $H^1$ torsor. This is a complex Fredholm index, not a real KO index.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold and $V$ a graded Hermitian Clifford module with compatible connection as in [[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]]. Use $R(X,Y)=[
abla^{LC}_X,
abla^{LC}_Y]-
abla^{LC}_{[X,Y]}$ and $\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=g(R(X,Y)Z,W)$. In a local oriented orthonormal frame define
$$F^S_{ij}= rac14\sum_{a,b}\operatorname{Rm}(e_i,e_j,e_a,e_b)c(e^a)c(e^b),\qquad F^{V/S}_{ij}=F^V_{ij}-F^S_{ij}.$$
Then $F^{V/S}_{ij}$ commutes with Clifford multiplication and
$$D_V^2=(
abla^V)^*
abla^V+ rac{\operatorname{scal}_g}{4}I+\sum_{i<j}c(e^i)c(e^j)F^{V/S}_{ij}.$$
In particular $D_V^2$ is formally symmetric Laplace type with positive-frequency principal symbol $|\xi|^2I$.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $TS^2$ admits a Spin lift; fix one. The unit sphere has area $4\pi$, so $\omega=(4\pi)^{-1}\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. On north and south charts define unitary connection forms $A_N=-\frac{ik}{2}(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ and $A_S=\frac{ik}{2}(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$. They extend smoothly over their respective poles, and $A_S-A_N=ik\,d\phi=g^{-1}dg$ for the unitary transition $g(\phi)=e^{ik\phi}$. Hence they define a Hermitian line bundle connection; differentiation gives $F=dA_N=dA_S=-(ik/2)\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=-2\pi i k\omega$.

By [F3]–[F5], the real Chern class of this connection integrates to $k$, so its integral first Chern class is $c_1(L_k)=kx$; the integral group is torsion-free by [F5], so its image in real cohomology determines it. The line-bundle curvature term in [F4] is $c(e^1)c(e^2)F_{12}=c(e^1)c(e^2)(-ik/2)=-\frac{k}{2}\Gamma$, because $\Gamma=i\,c(e^1)c(e^2)$. This is nonzero when $k\ne0$.

In dimension two $\widehat A$ has only its degree-zero term $1$, while $\operatorname{tr}\exp(-F/(2\pi i))=1+k\omega$ because $\omega^2=0$. Applying [F4] yields $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}(D^+_{S\otimes L_k})=\int_{S^2}k\omega=k$. For $k=0$ both the curvature term and index vanish. The construction is smooth at both poles by the displayed vanishing factors, the orientation is the complex orientation, and the formula uses the same actual spin-module interface as [F4].
